q-waves-noted.text: Pathological Q waves noted. Continue the read or review it?

qrs.hint: QRS 110-119 ms with a bundle-branch shape = incomplete block; 120 ms or more = complete block (adults).

options.label: Under 120 ms with a normal shape
120 ms or more: rsR' in V1, broad S in I and V6
120 ms or more: broad notched R in I, aVL, V5-V6, QS or rS in V1

qrs.text: Step 5 - QRS duration and shape. What do you see?

r-1avb.cite: ESC 2021 cardiac pacing and CRT guidelines
r-1avb.detail:
- Usually AV-nodal; look for drugs (beta-blocker, verapamil/diltiazem, digoxin), vagal tone, inferior MI, Lyme carditis, rheumatic fever.
- No treatment by itself; pacing only for marked PR prolongation (over 300 ms) with symptoms resembling pacemaker syndrome.
- To finish the read, go back and choose 'Note it and continue'.
r-1avb.text: First-degree AV block (PR over 200 ms): every P conducted

r-aberrancy.cite: ESC 2022 ventricular arrhythmias and SCD guidelines
r-aberrancy.detail:
- Supports aberrancy: a typical RBBB/LBBB shape (rapid initial deflection), identical QRS on a previous sinus ECG, onset with a premature P.
- If any VT feature is present, or in doubt, treat as VT.
- Adenosine can be used diagnostically only in a **regular, monomorphic** wide tachycardia in a stable patient.
r-aberrancy.text: SVT with aberrant conduction is possible, but only call it aberrancy when the evidence is clear

r-af.detail:
- No P waves, fibrillatory baseline, irregularly irregular RR.
- Unstable: synchronised cardioversion.
- Stable: rate control (beta-blocker, diltiazem/verapamil if LVEF > 40%, digoxin), anticoagulation by CHA2DS2-VA, rhythm control when symptomatic or early in the disease.
- Very fast, wide and irregular: think **pre-excited AF** (WPW) - no AV-nodal blockers.
- To finish the read, go back and choose 'Note it and continue'.
r-af.text: Atrial fibrillation: rate control, rhythm decision and anticoagulation by CHA2DS2-VA

r-avnrt.detail:
- Regular narrow tachycardia 140-250/min, P hidden in or just after the QRS (RP under 70 ms): pseudo-S in II, III, aVF and pseudo-r' in V1.
- Acute: modified Valsalva, then IV adenosine; IV verapamil/diltiazem or a beta-blocker if needed; synchronised cardioversion if unstable.
- Long term: catheter ablation of the slow pathway (cure over 95%).
r-avnrt.text: AVNRT (typical slow-fast): vagal manoeuvres, then adenosine

r-avrt.detail:
- Retrograde P in the ST segment, RP 70 ms or more (and RP shorter than PR); QRS narrow (antegrade down the AV node).
- Sinus-rhythm ECG shows pre-excitation only if the pathway is manifest (normal with a concealed pathway).
- Acute treatment as for AVNRT; ablation of the pathway is the definitive treatment.
- Wide-complex antidromic AVRT looks like VT.
r-avrt.text: Orthodromic AVRT (accessory pathway): vagal manoeuvres, adenosine; look for pre-excitation in sinus rhythm

r-cardiovert.cite: ESC 2022 ventricular arrhythmias and SCD guidelines
r-cardiovert.detail:
- Pulseless: defibrillate (ALS algorithm).
- With a pulse but shock, syncope, ischaemia or acute heart failure: sedation and synchronised cardioversion now; do not delay for a full 12-lead analysis.
- Afterwards: 12-lead in sinus rhythm, electrolytes, ischaemia work-up.
r-cardiovert.text: Unstable wide-complex tachycardia: immediate synchronised DC cardioversion

r-chb.cite: ESC 2021 cardiac pacing and CRT guidelines
r-chb.detail:
- P-P regular and R-R regular but unrelated; atrial rate higher than ventricular rate.
- Narrow escape (40-60/min) = junctional; wide escape (20-40/min) = ventricular, less stable.
- Look for reversible causes (inferior MI, drugs, hyperkalaemia, Lyme).
- Temporary pacing if unstable (isoprenaline or adrenaline as a bridge); permanent pacing for non-reversible block.
r-chb.text: Complete (third-degree) AV block: AV dissociation with a slow escape - pacing

r-dewinter.cite: de Winter RJ et al., N Engl J Med 2008
r-dewinter.detail:
- 1-3 mm upsloping ST depression at the J point in V1-V6 running into tall symmetric T waves; often 0.5-1 mm ST elevation in aVR; QRS not widened.
- Does not meet the classic STEMI millimetre criteria; recognise the pattern.
r-dewinter.text: de Winter pattern: proximal LAD occlusion - treat as a STEMI equivalent (immediate angiography)

r-dominant-r.cite: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 recommendations for the standardization and interpretation of the ECG
r-dominant-r.detail:
- With right axis and RV strain: RVH (pulmonary hypertension, PS, congenital).
- With ST depression and upright T in V1-V3: **posterior MI** - record V7-V9.
- With a delta wave: pre-excitation.
- Normal in children.
- To finish the read, go back and choose 'Note it and continue'.
r-dominant-r.text: Dominant R in V1: RVH, RBBB, posterior MI, WPW (left-sided pathway), HCM, dextrocardia, lead misplacement

r-extreme.cite: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 recommendations for the standardization and interpretation of the ECG
r-extreme.detail:
- In a wide-complex tachycardia, a northwest axis strongly favours VT.
- In sinus rhythm: check lead placement first, then RVH, congenital heart disease, paced rhythm.
- To finish the read, go back and choose 'Note it and continue'.
r-extreme.text: Extreme axis (northwest, -90 to 180): think VT, lead reversal, severe RV hypertrophy, hyperkalaemia

r-flutter.detail:
- Negative sawtooth F waves in II, III, aVF, positive in V1, atrial rate about 300/min; 2:1 conduction gives a regular rate near **150/min**; 4:1 gives about 75/min; variable block gives an irregular rhythm.
- Rate control is harder than in AF; cardioversion (often low energy) or CTI ablation (first-line for recurrent typical flutter).
- Anticoagulate as for AF.

r-hyperacute.cite: Fourth Universal Definition of MI (2018); ESC 2023 ACS guidelines
r-hyperacute.detail:
- Broad-based, tall, symmetric T waves, large relative to the QRS, confined to a territory; may precede ST elevation.
- Differs from hyperkalaemia (narrow-based, tented, diffuse, short QT).
- Serial ECGs, compare with old tracings, early cardiology/cath-lab discussion if pain continues.
r-hyperacute.text: Hyperacute T waves: possible early coronary occlusion - repeat the ECG every 15-30 minutes and treat as STEMI-equivalent if symptoms persist

r-hyperk.cite: KDIGO and UK Kidney Association hyperkalaemia guidance; Goldberger's Clinical Electrocardiography
r-hyperk.detail:
- Sequence as potassium rises: peaked T, then flat P and long PR, then wide QRS, then sine wave, VF or asystole (correlation with the exact level is poor).
- ECG changes = emergency: IV calcium (membrane stabilisation), insulin-glucose and salbutamol (shift), then removal (binders, dialysis).
r-hyperk.text: Hyperkalaemia until proven otherwise: check potassium now; if hyperkalaemia is confirmed (or strongly suspected) with any ECG change, give IV calcium first

r-hypok.cite: Goldberger's Clinical Electrocardiography; Braunwald's Heart Disease
r-hypok.detail:
- The T and U waves can fuse into an apparent long QT (really QU).
- Raises the risk of torsades and digoxin toxicity: replace potassium and magnesium.
r-hypok.text: Hypokalaemia pattern: flat T waves, ST depression, prominent U waves

r-ivcd.cite: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 recommendations for the standardization and interpretation of the ECG
r-ivcd.detail:
- Check potassium and drugs (tricyclics, class Ic, cocaine) urgently.
- Look for pacing spikes and a delta wave.
- Non-specific intraventricular conduction delay is common in dilated cardiomyopathy.
- To finish the read, go back and choose 'Note it and continue'.
r-ivcd.text: Wide QRS without a typical bundle-branch pattern: think hyperkalaemia, sodium-channel drugs, pacing, pre-excitation, cardiomyopathy

r-lad.cite: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 recommendations for the standardization and interpretation of the ECG
r-lad.detail:
- **Left anterior fascicular block** (axis -45 to -90, qR in aVL, rS in II, III, aVF, QRS under 120 ms).
- Inferior MI (Q waves in II, III, aVF), LVH, LBBB, RV apical pacing, WPW (some pathways), ostium primum ASD, hyperkalaemia.
- To finish the read, go back and choose 'Note it and continue'.

r-lbbb.cite: Sgarbossa EB et al. N Engl J Med 1996; Smith SW et al. Ann Emerg Med 2012; ESC 2023 ACS guidelines
r-lbbb.detail:
- QRS 120 ms or more, broad notched R in I, aVL, V5-V6, no septal q, QS or rS in V1, discordant ST-T.
- Almost always structural disease: echo for LV function; LBBB with symptomatic HF, LVEF 35% or less despite optimal therapy and QRS 130 ms or more can qualify for CRT (class I at 150 ms or more).
- Acute chest pain: concordant ST elevation 1 mm or more, concordant ST depression 1 mm or more in V1-V3, or disproportionate discordant ST elevation suggest occlusion MI.
- To finish the read, go back and choose 'Note it and continue'.
r-lbbb.text: Complete left bundle branch block: ST-T changes are secondary - use Sgarbossa criteria for ischaemia

r-long-qt.cite: ESC 2022 ventricular arrhythmias and SCD guidelines
r-long-qt.detail:
- QTc 500 ms or more (or a rise of 60 ms or more on a drug) = high risk of torsades de pointes.
- Causes: drugs (class Ia/III antiarrhythmics, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, antipsychotics, methadone, ondansetron), hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypocalcaemia, bradycardia, congenital LQTS.
- Torsades: IV magnesium; temporary pacing or isoprenaline to raise the rate.
r-long-qt.text: Long QT: stop QT-prolonging drugs, correct potassium and magnesium, look for congenital LQTS

r-long-rp.detail:
- RP longer than PR.
- Atrial tachycardia: P shape differs from sinus; continues despite AV block after adenosine.
- Atypical (fast-slow) AVNRT and PJRT: deeply negative P in II, III, aVF.
- Incessant tachycardia can cause tachycardiomyopathy.
r-long-rp.text: Long-RP tachycardia: atrial tachycardia, atypical AVNRT or PJRT

r-low-voltage.cite: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 recommendations for the standardization and interpretation of the ECG
r-low-voltage.detail:
- Low voltage + tachycardia + **electrical alternans** = pericardial effusion with tamponade until proven otherwise: urgent echo.
- Low voltage with an echocardiographically thick LV = **cardiac amyloidosis** (voltage-mass mismatch).
- To finish the read, go back and choose 'Note it and continue'.
r-low-voltage.text: Low QRS voltage: effusion, infiltration, obesity, emphysema, hypothyroidism

r-lvh.cite: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 recommendations for the standardization and interpretation of the ECG
r-lvh.detail:
- Sokolow-Lyon: S V1 + R V5 or V6 35 mm or more. Cornell: R aVL + S V3 over 28 mm (men), over 20 mm (women).
- Supportive: strain (downsloping ST depression with asymmetric T inversion in I, aVL, V5-V6), left atrial enlargement, left axis.
- Voltage criteria are specific but insensitive; echo or CMR confirms.
- To finish the read, go back and choose 'Note it and continue'.
r-lvh.text: LV hypertrophy by voltage: look for strain and left atrial enlargement; confirm with echo

r-mat.detail:
- Rate over 100/min, three or more P-wave morphologies, variable PR and RR.
- Classic in COPD exacerbation, hypoxia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, theophylline.
- Cardioversion does not work; correct the cause; magnesium, verapamil or a beta-blocker (if lung disease allows) for rate.
r-mat.text: Multifocal atrial tachycardia: treat the underlying lung disease, hypoxia and electrolytes

r-mobitz1.cite: ESC 2021 cardiac pacing and CRT guidelines
r-mobitz1.detail:
- PR lengthens, RR shortens, then a non-conducted P; the pause is less than two PP intervals; grouped beating.
- Causes: high vagal tone, athletes, sleep, inferior MI, AV-nodal drugs.
- Treat the cause; atropine if symptomatic; pacing only if symptomatic or shown to be infranodal.
r-mobitz1.text: Second-degree AV block, Mobitz I (Wenckebach): usually AV-nodal and benign

r-mobitz2.cite: ESC 2021 cardiac pacing and CRT guidelines
r-mobitz2.detail:
- Fixed PR before and after the dropped beat; QRS is often wide (bundle-branch disease).
- Risk of sudden complete block with a slow, unreliable ventricular escape.
- Transcutaneous pacing ready; atropine may not work (and can increase the block); **permanent pacing is indicated even without symptoms** once reversible causes are excluded.
- 2:1 block cannot be classed as Mobitz I or II from one strip: a wide QRS, or no improvement with atropine/exercise, favours an infranodal level.
r-mobitz2.text: Second-degree AV block, Mobitz II (or 2:1 block of uncertain level): treat as infranodal until proven otherwise - admit, monitor and plan pacing

r-normal.cite: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 recommendations for the standardization and interpretation of the ECG
r-normal.detail:
- Summarise: rhythm and rate, axis, intervals (PR, QRS, QTc), morphology, ST-T, and the comparison with any old ECG.
- A normal ECG does not exclude ACS: repeat it if symptoms recur.
r-normal.text: Normal ECG for age (or no further abnormality): write the conclusion

r-paced.cite: ESC 2021 cardiac pacing and CRT guidelines
r-paced.detail:
- Atrial spike then P; ventricular spike then a wide QRS.
- RV apical pacing gives an LBBB-like QRS with a superior (left) axis.
- Failure to capture: spike without a following complex. Failure to sense (undersensing): spikes falling regardless of intrinsic beats.
- Ischaemia in a paced rhythm: concordant ST changes, or disproportionately discordant ST elevation (Smith-modified Sgarbossa).
r-paced.text: Paced rhythm: check capture and sensing; read ST changes with modified Sgarbossa criteria

r-pericarditis.cite: ESC 2025 myocarditis and pericarditis guidelines; ESC 2015 pericardial diseases guidelines; Braunwald's Heart Disease
r-pericarditis.detail:
- Diffuse concave ST elevation (not in a coronary territory), PR depression, ST depression and PR elevation in aVR; no Q waves; no reciprocal ST depression except aVR/V1.
- Spodick sign (downsloping TP segment); ST/T ratio in V6 over 0.25 favours pericarditis over early repolarisation.
- Exclude myocardial involvement (troponin) and tamponade (echo).
r-pericarditis.text: Acute pericarditis pattern: echo for effusion; NSAID or aspirin plus colchicine

r-polymorphic-vt.cite: ESC 2022 ventricular arrhythmias and SCD guidelines
r-polymorphic-vt.detail:
- Sustained polymorphic VT is rarely tolerated: unsynchronised shock (defibrillation energy), ALS if pulseless.
- **Long QTc (torsades de pointes)**: IV magnesium, correct potassium, stop QT-prolonging drugs; isoprenaline or temporary pacing for pause-dependent torsades.
- **Normal QTc**: acute ischaemia until proven otherwise - urgent angiography; also consider CPVT, Brugada syndrome and short QT.
r-polymorphic-vt.text: Polymorphic VT: defibrillate if sustained or pulseless, then check the QTc - torsades de pointes (long QT) or ischaemic polymorphic VT (normal QT)

r-posterior.detail:
- Mirror image of posterior injury: ST depression maximal in V1-V3 (0.5 mm or more), tall broad R, upright T.
- V7-V9: 0.5 mm or more (1 mm or more in men under 40) = STEMI equivalent (usually LCx or RCA).
- Treat on the primary PCI pathway; often accompanies inferior or lateral STEMI.
r-posterior.text: Posterior STEMI until proven otherwise: record V7-V9 (ST elevation 0.5 mm or more confirms)

r-preexcited-af.detail:
- Irregular, very fast (can exceed 250/min), QRS width varying beat to beat ("FBI": fast, broad, irregular).
- Adenosine, verapamil/diltiazem, beta-blockers and digoxin can speed conduction down the pathway and cause VF.
- Unstable: synchronised cardioversion. Stable: IV procainamide or ibutilide, then pathway ablation.
- IV amiodarone is not recommended (ESC 2019, class III).
r-preexcited-af.text: Pre-excited AF (WPW): no AV-nodal blockers - cardiovert or give IV procainamide/ibutilide

r-q-waves.detail:
- 4th UDMI: any Q in V2-V3 of 20 ms or more, or QS in V2-V3; elsewhere Q of 30 ms or more and 1 mm deep (or QS) in two contiguous leads of a group (I, aVL; II, III, aVF; V4-V6).
- Mimics: LBBB, WPW, HCM (septal Q), lead misplacement, cardiomyopathy.
- Persistent ST elevation weeks after anterior MI with Q waves suggests an LV aneurysm.
- To finish the read, go back and choose 'Note it and continue'.
r-q-waves.text: Pathological Q waves: prior (or evolving) transmural infarction in that territory

r-rad.cite: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 recommendations for the standardization and interpretation of the ECG
r-rad.detail:
- RV hypertrophy or strain (pulmonary hypertension, PE, COPD), lateral MI, **left posterior fascicular block** (diagnosis of exclusion), lead reversal, dextrocardia, ostium secundum ASD, normal in children and tall thin adults.
- To finish the read, go back and choose 'Note it and continue'.

r-rbbb.cite: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 recommendations for the standardization and interpretation of the ECG
r-rbbb.detail:
- QRS 120 ms or more; secondary T inversion in V1-V3 is expected.
- Causes: normal variant, RV strain (PE), ischaemia, congenital heart disease (ASD), degenerative conduction disease.
- STEMI can still be diagnosed with RBBB; RBBB with ongoing ischaemic symptoms is managed like STEMI (ESC 2023).
- RBBB + left anterior fascicular block = bifascicular block.
- To finish the read, go back and choose 'Note it and continue'.
r-rbbb.text: Complete right bundle branch block: rsR' in V1, broad S in I and V6

r-reversal.cite: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 recommendations for the standardization and interpretation of the ECG
r-reversal.detail:
- **LA/RA reversal**: I inverted, II and III swapped, aVR and aVL swapped; the **precordial leads are normal** (R waves grow from V1 to V5).
- **Dextrocardia**: I inverted as well, but the R waves **shrink** from V1 to V6; repeat with right-sided chest leads.
- Recheck the electrodes and record again before reading axis or ST.
r-reversal.text: Suspect limb-lead reversal (LA/RA swap) or dextrocardia; repeat the ECG before interpreting

r-short-pr.cite: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 recommendations for the standardization and interpretation of the ECG
r-short-pr.detail:
- Check the P axis: inverted P in II, III, aVF = low atrial or junctional origin.
- With an upright sinus P it is usually a normal variant (enhanced AV-nodal conduction).
- To finish the read, go back and choose 'Note it and continue'.
r-short-pr.text: Short PR without a delta wave: ectopic low-atrial or junctional rhythm, or a normal variant

r-sinus-tach.detail:
- Pain, fever, hypovolaemia, anaemia, sepsis, hypoxia, PE, thyrotoxicosis, heart failure, drugs.
- Do not rate-control a compensatory tachycardia.
- To finish the read, go back and choose 'Note it and continue'.
r-sinus-tach.text: Sinus tachycardia: find and treat the cause

r-sinus-tach-wide.cite: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 recommendations for the standardization and interpretation of the ECG
r-sinus-tach-wide.detail:
- Confirm 1:1 AV relation with a constant PR across the strip; compare the QRS with an old ECG.
- If P waves are uncertain, fall back to 'treat as VT'.
r-sinus-tach-wide.text: Sinus tachycardia with a wide QRS (bundle-branch block, pre-excitation or pacing): treat the cause of the tachycardia, not the QRS

r-slow-escape.cite: ESC 2021 cardiac pacing and CRT guidelines
r-slow-escape.detail:
- Regular narrow escape without P (or retrograde P) = junctional rhythm.
- Slow irregular rhythm without P = AF with slow ventricular response (AV-nodal drugs, digoxin toxicity, conduction disease).
- Check potassium, digoxin level, drugs, ischaemia and thyroid function; pace if symptomatic and irreversible.
r-slow-escape.text: Slow rhythm without P waves: junctional or ventricular escape, slow AF, or sinus arrest - find the cause

r-std.cite: Fourth Universal Definition of MI (2018); ACC/AHA 2025 ACS guideline, Table 3
r-std.detail:
- New horizontal or downsloping ST depression 0.5 mm or more in two contiguous leads = ischaemia (UDMI).
- **Widespread ST depression with ST elevation in aVR** (often with ST elevation in V1): left main or three-vessel ischaemia (or global subendocardial ischaemia) - high risk, urgent angiography.
- Serial ECGs, hs-troponin; reciprocal depression may be the mirror of a STEMI elsewhere.
r-std.text: ST depression: NSTE-ACS until proven otherwise; also strain, digoxin, hypokalaemia, rate-related

r-ste-mimic.cite: Wang K, Asinger RW, Marriott HJ. N Engl J Med 2003 (ST elevation other than MI); ESC 2022 ventricular arrhythmias and SCD guidelines (Brugada)
r-ste-mimic.detail:
- **Benign early repolarisation**: concave ST elevation mainly V2-V5 with a J-point notch or slur, no reciprocal depression, stable on repeat ECGs; ST/T ratio in V6 under 0.25.
- **LV aneurysm**: persistent ST elevation with QS waves in an old infarct territory weeks after MI; T waves small relative to the QRS.
- **LVH**: ST elevation in V1-V3 discordant to deep S waves and proportionate to the voltage, with lateral strain.
- **Brugada pattern**: coved ST elevation of 2 mm or more in V1-V2 with a negative T (type 1) or a saddle-back (type 2); ask about syncope, fever and family history.
- Ongoing chest pain or doubt: serial ECGs, troponin and early cardiology discussion.
r-ste-mimic.text: ST elevation without an occlusion pattern: early repolarisation, LV aneurysm, LVH or Brugada pattern - compare with old ECGs and repeat if symptoms continue

r-stemi.cite: Fourth Universal Definition of MI (2018); ACC/AHA 2025 ACS guideline, Table 3
r-stemi.detail:
- Territory: V1-V4 anterior (LAD), II/III/aVF inferior (RCA or LCx), I/aVL/V5-V6 lateral (LCx or diagonal).
- Inferior STEMI with ST elevation III over II: RCA - record V3R/V4R for RV infarction (avoid nitrates).
- Aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitor and anticoagulation per protocol; fibrinolysis if PCI cannot be achieved within 120 minutes.
r-stemi.text: STEMI: activate the reperfusion pathway (primary PCI if achievable within 120 minutes of diagnosis)

r-t-inversion.cite: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 recommendations for the standardization and interpretation of the ECG
r-t-inversion.detail:
- Normal: aVR, often V1, sometimes III; V1-V3 in children and some adults of Black African descent (juvenile pattern).
- Ischaemia (symmetric, territorial), LVH strain (asymmetric, lateral), RV strain/PE (V1-V4 with inferior leads), HCM (deep apical), post-tachycardia or memory T waves, raised intracranial pressure (giant inverted T), Takotsubo.
- Compare with old ECGs and repeat.
r-t-inversion.text: T-wave inversion: interpret by territory, shape and context

r-vt.cite: ESC 2022 ventricular arrhythmias and SCD guidelines
r-vt.detail:
- VT clues: AV dissociation, capture/fusion beats, precordial concordance, initial R in aVR, RS interval over 100 ms in a precordial lead, very wide QRS, northwest axis.
- Stable: synchronised cardioversion if sedation risk is low; otherwise IV procainamide or amiodarone.
- Avoid verapamil/diltiazem in an undiagnosed wide tachycardia.
- Look for structural heart disease (echo, ischaemia).
r-vt.text: Treat as ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise

r-wellens.cite: de Zwaan C, Bar FW, Wellens HJ. Am Heart J 1982; ESC 2023 ACS guidelines
r-wellens.detail:
- Type A: biphasic T (up then down) in V2-V3. Type B: deep symmetric T inversion in V2-V3 (can extend V1-V6).
- Appears in the pain-free period; little or no ST elevation, no pathological Q waves, R waves preserved.
- High risk of extensive anterior MI: admit, treat as NSTE-ACS, invasive strategy.
r-wellens.text: Wellens pattern: critical proximal LAD stenosis - no stress test; early angiography

r-wpw.detail:
- PR under 120 ms, slurred upstroke (delta), QRS usually over 110 ms, secondary ST-T changes.
- Delta polarity localises the pathway (negative in I/aVL with positive V1 = left lateral).
- Symptoms (AVRT, pre-excited AF) or high-risk features: refer for EP study and ablation.
- Pre-excitation can mimic infarction (pseudo-Q) or hypertrophy.
r-wpw.text: Ventricular pre-excitation (WPW pattern): short PR, delta wave, wide QRS

options.label: Review the causes of right axis deviation

rad.text: Right axis deviation noted. Continue the read or review the causes?

rate.hint: Regular rhythm: 300 / number of large squares between R waves (or 1500 / small squares). Irregular: QRS count in the 10 s strip x 6.
rate.text: Step 1 - Rate. What is the ventricular rate?

options.label: Note it and continue: ST segment (STEMI criteria still apply in RBBB)

rbbb-noted.text: Right bundle branch block noted. Continue the read or review it?

rhythm.hint: Sinus P waves are upright in I, II and aVF and inverted in aVR (P axis 0 to +75 degrees).

options.label: Upright P in I and II before every QRS, constant PR: sinus rhythm
Irregularly irregular, no P waves, fibrillatory baseline
Sawtooth flutter waves (about 300/min) with 3:1, 4:1 or variable conduction
P waves present but not every P is followed by a QRS
Pacing spikes before the P waves and/or the QRS complexes

rhythm.text: Step 2 - Rhythm at a normal rate. What is the relation of P waves to QRS complexes?

short-pr-noted.text: Short PR without a delta wave noted. Continue the read or review it?

sinus-tach-noted.text: Sinus tachycardia noted. Continue the read or review it?

st.hint: Measure at the J point against the TP (or PR) baseline and compare with any previous ECG.

options.label: ST depression maximal in V1-V3 with tall R and upright T waves
Upsloping ST depression running into tall symmetric T waves in V1-V6
Horizontal or downsloping ST depression elsewhere (with or without ST elevation in aVR)

st.text: Step 7 - ST segment (at the J point, against the TP or PR baseline). What is it?

ste.hint: STEMI thresholds: 1 mm or more in all leads except V2-V3; in V2-V3 2 mm (men 40 y or older), 2.5 mm (men under 40), 1.5 mm (women).

options.label: In 2 contiguous leads of a coronary territory, meeting STEMI thresholds, often with reciprocal depression
Diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression; ST depression only in aVR (and V1)
Not in a coronary pattern or below thresholds (early repolarisation, LV aneurysm, LVH, Brugada)

ste.text: ST elevation. What is its pattern?

tall-t.hint: Hyperkalaemic T: narrow base, pointed ('tented'), diffuse. Hyperacute T: broad base, bulky, large relative to the QRS, confined to a territory.

options.label: Tall, narrow-based, symmetric, tented T waves, diffuse (not one territory), often with a short QT
Broad-based, bulky, symmetric T waves in a coronary territory (often with reciprocal change), with chest pain

tall-t.text: Tall T waves. What shape and distribution?

tw.hint: QTc = QT / square root of RR (Bazett, in seconds); Fridericia (QT / cube root of RR) is better at fast or slow rates. Measure QT in II or V5 to the end of T (tangent method).

options.label: T upright except aVR (III and V1 may be negative), QTc normal
Deep symmetric or biphasic T inversion in V2-V3 in a pain-free patient after chest pain
Long QTc (450 ms or more in men, 460 ms or more in women)
Flat T waves with prominent U waves

tw.text: Step 8 - T waves and QT. Which applies?

unstable.text: Wide-complex tachycardia. Is the patient haemodynamically unstable (shock, syncope, ischaemic chest pain, acute heart failure)?

options.label: Normal voltage, normal R-wave progression, no pathological Q waves
Tall voltage: S V1 + R V5/V6 35 mm or more, or R aVL + S V3 over 28 mm (men) / 20 mm (women)
Dominant R wave in V1 (R/S over 1)
Low voltage: under 5 mm in every limb lead or under 10 mm in every precordial lead
Pathological Q waves in two contiguous leads

voltage.text: Step 6 - QRS voltage, R-wave progression and Q waves. Which applies?

wide-features.hint: Brugada (1991) and Vereckei aVR (2008) algorithms; about 80% of all wide tachycardias are VT, over 90% with prior MI or structural heart disease.

options.label: AV dissociation, capture/fusion beats, precordial concordance or an initial R wave in aVR
Polymorphic QRS twisting around the baseline
Irregular, very fast, QRS width varying beat to beat
A sinus P wave before every QRS at a constant PR (sinus tachycardia with BBB, pre-excitation or pacing)
Typical RBBB or LBBB shape identical to a previous sinus ECG
None of these clear-cut / not sure

wide-features.text: Stable wide-complex tachycardia. Which feature is present?

width.hint: Measure in the lead where the QRS looks widest; 120 ms = 3 small squares.
width.text: Tachycardia. How wide is the QRS?

ecg-systematic-reading-algorithm.alt_text: Decision tree for reading an ECG systematically. Step 0 checks calibration, paper speed and lead placement (lead I inverted suggests limb-lead reversal or dextrocardia; non-standard calibration means rescaling every measurement). Step 1 sorts the rate into under 60, 60-100 and over 100 per minute. Slow rates and abnormal rhythms go to an AV-relationship question that separates sinus bradycardia, first-degree block, Mobitz I, Mobitz II or 2:1 block, complete heart block and escape rhythms; atrial flutter with 3:1, 4:1 or variable conduction can be chosen at a normal rate. Fast rates split by QRS width: narrow tachycardias into AF, flutter (regular or with variable block), multifocal atrial tachycardia, sinus tachycardia, AVNRT, AVRT and long-RP tachycardia by regularity and P-wave position; wide tachycardias into immediate cardioversion if unstable, otherwise VT (the default), polymorphic VT, pre-excited AF, sinus tachycardia with a wide QRS or aberrancy. Findings met on the way (AF, sinus tachycardia, first-degree block, extreme axis, short PR, bundle-branch blocks, LVH, dominant R in V1, low voltage, Q waves) can be noted so that the read continues, or reviewed. The read continues through axis (left, right, extreme deviation), PR interval (WPW, short PR, first-degree block), QRS (RBBB, LBBB, non-specific delay), voltage and Q waves, ST segment (STEMI, pericarditis, non-ischaemic ST elevation, posterior MI, de Winter, ST depression) and T waves and QT (hyperkalaemia versus hyperacute T waves, Wellens, long QT, hypokalaemia, other T inversion) to a final conclusion.
ecg-systematic-reading-algorithm.attribution: Original decision tree for this study aid, based on the AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 ECG standardization recommendations, the Fourth Universal Definition of MI, ACC/AHA 2025 ACS, ESC 2019 SVT, ESC 2021 pacing, ESC 2022 ventricular arrhythmia and ESC 2024 AF guidelines.
ecg-systematic-reading-algorithm.caption: Step through a 12-lead ECG in a fixed order: technique, rate, rhythm (and AV relation), axis, PR, QRS, voltage and Q waves, ST segment, T waves and QT. Findings met on the way (AF, sinus tachycardia, first-degree block, extreme axis, short PR, bundle-branch blocks, hypertrophy, Q waves) can be noted so the read continues to the ST and T steps, or opened for review; tachycardias branch into narrow and wide pathways, and ST/T findings end in their differential and next action. Study aid based on the cited guidelines; verify against the current full guideline before clinical use.
ecg-systematic-reading-algorithm.title: Systematic ECG reading: rate, rhythm, axis, intervals, morphology, ST-T

ecg-vt-strip.alt_text: Schematic 8-second lead II rhythm strip of monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. Regular, wide (about 160 ms), identical QRS complexes at 170 per minute, mainly negative in lead II, with broad T waves of opposite polarity. Dissociated sinus P waves at 75 per minute are labelled P with arrows; they fall at different points of the cycle (on the T wave, between complexes, inside the QRS), deforming the trace, and bear no fixed relation to the QRS complexes: AV dissociation.
ecg-vt-strip.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
ecg-vt-strip.caption: Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia at 170/min with AV dissociation (lead II): P waves (marked P) march through at their own slower rate. Schematic, not a real tracing.
ecg-vt-strip.title: Monomorphic VT 170/min with AV dissociation (lead II)

ecg-wellens-12-lead.alt_text: Schematic 12-lead ECG of the Wellens pattern (type B) in sinus rhythm at 68 per minute. Deep, symmetric T-wave inversion in V2 and V3, less deep in V4 and shallow in V1. R waves in V1-V4 are preserved (normal R-wave progression), there are no pathological Q waves and the ST segments are isoelectric. Limb leads and V5-V6 are normal.
ecg-wellens-12-lead.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
ecg-wellens-12-lead.caption: Wellens pattern, type B: deep symmetric T-wave inversion in V2-V3 with preserved R waves, no Q waves and an isoelectric ST segment - a warning of critical proximal LAD stenosis. Schematic, not a real tracing.
ecg-wellens-12-lead.title: 12-lead ECG: Wellens pattern, type B (deep symmetric T inversion V2-V3)

ecg-wpw-12-lead.alt_text: Schematic 12-lead ECG in sinus rhythm at 75 per minute showing pre-excitation. The PR interval is short (100 ms) and the QRS starts with a slurred upstroke (delta wave), making the QRS wide (about 140 ms). The delta wave is negative in I and aVL (pseudo-Q waves) and positive in V1-V3 and the inferior leads, the pattern of a left lateral accessory pathway. T waves are small (secondary repolarisation change).
ecg-wpw-12-lead.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
ecg-wpw-12-lead.caption: Ventricular pre-excitation (WPW pattern), left lateral accessory pathway: short PR, delta wave and wide QRS. Schematic, not a real tracing.
ecg-wpw-12-lead.title: 12-lead ECG: ventricular pre-excitation (WPW pattern), left lateral pathway

echo-a2c-view.alt_text: Schematic apical two-chamber view with the apex at the top: only the LV and the LA are seen. The inferior wall is on the left of the screen and the anterior wall on the right; the mitral valve is open in diastole. The left atrial appendage arises beside the anterior side of the LA, and the coronary sinus is seen in cross-section in the left atrioventricular groove next to the inferior wall. Normal anatomy.
echo-a2c-view.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
echo-a2c-view.caption: Apical two-chamber view: LV and LA only, with the inferior wall on the left and the anterior wall on the right of the screen; the second plane of the biplane Simpson method and the view of the left atrial appendage from the apex. Schematic, not a real recording.

echo-a4c-view.alt_text: Schematic apical four-chamber view in the ASE orientation with the apex at the top: the LV on the right of the screen and the RV on the left, the atria at the bottom (LA right, RA left), separated by the interventricular and interatrial septa. The RV is smaller and triangular, with a moderator band near its apex; its apex meets the septum well below the LV apex (about two-thirds of the LV length), so the LV alone forms the cardiac apex. Both atrioventricular valves are open in diastole; the septal tricuspid leaflet inserts slightly closer to the apex than the anterior mitral leaflet (the normal apical offset). The lateral LV wall is labelled and pulmonary veins enter the LA. Normal anatomy.
echo-a4c-view.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
echo-a4c-view.caption: Apical four-chamber view in the ASE orientation (apex at the top, LV on the right of the screen). The view for chamber size and function, AV-valve inflow and regurgitation, and RV size; the normal RV is about two-thirds of the LV length and does not reach the apex; the septal tricuspid leaflet inserts slightly nearer the apex than the mitral leaflet. Schematic, not a real recording.

echo-ar-pht-severe.alt_text: Schematic continuous-wave Doppler from the apical five-chamber window with a reference ECG, heart rate 55 per minute. A dense diastolic jet above the baseline (towards the transducer) starts at aortic closure at about 4.5 m/s and decelerates steeply, reaching about 1 m/s by end-diastole; systolic forward flow of about 1.5 m/s lies below the baseline. Calipers mark the pressure half-time (from Vpeak to Vpeak divided by the square root of 2) of 170 ms, and a dashed line extends the early slope to the baseline. Footer: pressure half-time 170 ms. Finding: severe aortic regurgitation (pressure half-time under 200 ms).
echo-ar-pht-severe.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
echo-ar-pht-severe.caption: Continuous-wave Doppler of aortic regurgitation from the apex: a dense diastolic jet with a steep deceleration slope as aortic and LV diastolic pressures equalise quickly. Pressure half-time 170 ms: under 200 ms supports severe AR (ASE 2017; over 500 ms suggests mild AR). Schematic, not a real recording.
echo-ar-pht-severe.title: CW Doppler: severe aortic regurgitation (pressure half-time 170 ms)

echo-as-cw-severe.alt_text: Schematic continuous-wave Doppler spectrum from the apical five-chamber window with a reference ECG above. In each systole a jet lies below the baseline (flow away from the transducer): it starts at aortic opening after the QRS, has a full, rounded contour with its peak a little after mid-systole, and ends at aortic closure; a denser low-velocity LVOT envelope of about 1 m/s sits inside it. A dashed line marks the peak velocity, 4.6 m/s. Footer: Vmax 4.6 m/s, peak gradient 4V squared = 85 mmHg, mean gradient 50 mmHg. Finding: severe aortic stenosis.
echo-as-cw-severe.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
echo-as-cw-severe.caption: Continuous-wave Doppler across a severely stenotic aortic valve: a dense, rounded jet below the baseline that peaks late in systole, with the low-velocity LVOT signal inside it. Vmax 4.6 m/s, peak gradient 85 mmHg, mean gradient 50 mmHg: severe by ASE/EACVI 2017 and ESC/EACTS 2021 (Vmax at least 4 m/s, mean gradient at least 40 mmHg). Schematic, not a real recording.
echo-as-cw-severe.title: CW Doppler: severe valvular aortic stenosis (Vmax 4.6 m/s, mean gradient 50 mmHg)

check.hint: The e', E/e' and E/A criteria are validated in sinus rhythm with a native, non-diseased mitral valve. Interpret with care: LBBB or paced rhythm (septal e'), E-A fusion (sinus tachycardia, first-degree AV block), pre-capillary PH (TR velocity does not reflect LA pressure).

options.label: Sinus rhythm, no significant mitral valve disease, no other confounder
Any mitral stenosis, moderate or severe MR or annular calcification, mitral repair or prosthesis
Heart transplant, LVAD, or constrictive pericarditis suspected

check.text: Step 0 - Can the standard algorithms be applied?

e-vel.hint: A low E with E/A 0.8 or less means a normal LA pressure; a higher E needs the three criteria.
e-vel.text: E/A is 0.8 or less. What is the peak E velocity?

inflow.hint: Pulsed-wave Doppler at the leaflet tips in the apical four-chamber view.
inflow.text: Algorithm 2 - Diastolic dysfunction is present or expected. What is the mitral inflow E/A ratio?

lvef.hint: Algorithm 1 asks whether diastolic function is normal; algorithm 2 grades dysfunction and estimates LA pressure. In HCM, ASE 2016 uses four criteria instead (average E/e' > 14, Ar-A ≥ 30 ms, TR > 2.8 m/s, LAVI > 34 mL/m2; more than half positive = raised LA pressure).

options.label: LVEF normal and no myocardial disease
LVEF normal but myocardial disease (LVH, HCM, infiltrative disease, regional wall-motion abnormality)

lvef.text: Step 1 - Which algorithm? Is the LVEF reduced, or is there myocardial disease despite a normal LVEF?

r-a-indeterminate.cite: ASE/EACVI 2016 recommendations for the evaluation of LV diastolic function (Nagueh et al., JASE 2016)
r-a-indeterminate.detail:
- Half the criteria are abnormal: diastolic function **cannot be called normal or abnormal**.
- Report it as indeterminate; recheck the measurements (e' sampling site, TR alignment, LA tracing).
- Supplementary data: pulmonary vein S/D, LA strain, Valsalva response of the inflow, diastolic stress echo.
r-a-indeterminate.text: Indeterminate (exactly half of the criteria abnormal)

r-af.cite: ASE/EACVI 2016 recommendations for the evaluation of LV diastolic function (Nagueh et al., JASE 2016)
r-af.detail:
- There is no A wave, so E/A and the grading scheme do not apply; measure over several cycles (or index beats after two similar RR intervals).
- Supportive of raised filling pressure: septal E/e' 11 or more, TR velocity over 2.8 m/s, short mitral deceleration time (160 ms or less) in reduced LVEF, rapid early E acceleration, short IVRT.
- Integrate several parameters; one alone is unreliable.
r-af.text: Atrial fibrillation: use AF-specific indices, not the E/A-based algorithm

r-b-indeterminate.cite: ASE/EACVI 2016 recommendations for the evaluation of LV diastolic function (Nagueh et al., JASE 2016)
r-b-indeterminate.detail:
- Only one criterion is available, or the two available criteria disagree.
- Report the filling pressure as indeterminate. In reduced LVEF a pulmonary vein S/D ratio under 1 supports raised LA pressure; LA strain, Valsalva response or invasive measurement can also help.
r-b-indeterminate.text: LA pressure and grade cannot be determined

r-grade1.cite: ASE/EACVI 2016 recommendations for the evaluation of LV diastolic function (Nagueh et al., JASE 2016)
r-grade1.detail:
- Mitral inflow E/A 0.8 or less with E 50 cm/s or less, **or** at least 2 of the 3 criteria negative.
- **Normal mean LA pressure** (normal filling pressure at rest).
- Typical: hypertension with LVH, older age, early ischaemic heart disease.
r-grade1.text: Grade I diastolic dysfunction: impaired relaxation, normal LA pressure

r-grade2.cite: ASE/EACVI 2016 recommendations for the evaluation of LV diastolic function (Nagueh et al., JASE 2016)
r-grade2.detail:
- At least 2 of the 3 criteria positive (E/e' > 14, TR > 2.8 m/s, LAVI > 34 mL/m2), with E/A between 0.8 and 2 (or 0.8 or less with E over 50 cm/s).
- **Raised mean LA pressure (raised filling pressure)**.
- A fall in E/A of 50% or more with Valsalva supports a pseudonormal pattern.
r-grade2.text: Grade II diastolic dysfunction: raised LA pressure (pseudonormal filling)

r-grade3.cite: ASE/EACVI 2016 recommendations for the evaluation of LV diastolic function (Nagueh et al., JASE 2016)
r-grade3.detail:
- Mitral inflow E/A **2 or more** (short deceleration time, typically under 160 ms).
- **Markedly raised mean LA pressure**; poor prognosis, especially when it persists after decongestion.
- Typical: decompensated HFrEF, restrictive cardiomyopathy (for example amyloidosis).
r-grade3.text: Grade III diastolic dysfunction: restrictive filling, raised LA pressure

r-mitral.cite: ASE/EACVI 2016 recommendations for the evaluation of LV diastolic function (Nagueh et al., JASE 2016)
r-mitral.detail:
- MAC, mitral stenosis, significant MR, repair or prosthesis alter E, A and e' independently of LV relaxation.
- Use alternatives from the 2016 recommendations (for example IVRT, pulmonary vein Ar-A duration, the IVRT/TE-e' ratio) and interpret with caution.
r-mitral.text: Mitral valve disease or annular calcification: the e'-based criteria are invalid

r-normal.cite: ASE/EACVI 2016 recommendations for the evaluation of LV diastolic function (Nagueh et al., JASE 2016)
r-normal.detail:
- More than half of the available criteria are normal: **normal diastolic function and normal filling pressure**.
- An E/A under 1 in an older adult with normal e', E/e', TR velocity and LAVI is an age effect, not dysfunction.
- If symptoms suggest HFpEF despite normal resting indices, consider diastolic stress echo (exercise E/e' and TR velocity) or invasive testing.
r-normal.text: Normal diastolic function (fewer than half of the criteria abnormal)

r-other.cite: ASE/EACVI 2016 diastolic function recommendations; ASE 2013 pericardial disease recommendations
r-other.detail:
- Heart transplant: restrictive-looking inflow is common and not graded with the standard algorithm.
- LVAD: filling indices depend on pump speed.
- Constrictive pericarditis: preserved or increased medial e' despite raised filling pressure (annulus paradoxus) and lateral e' lower than medial (annulus reversus); E/e' is misleading. Look for septal bounce, respiratory variation of inflow and expiratory hepatic vein diastolic flow reversal.
r-other.text: Special population: interpret filling indices in context

echo-diastolic-function-algorithm.alt_text: Decision tree for echocardiographic assessment of diastolic function. Step 0 checks for confounders (atrial fibrillation, any mitral stenosis, moderate or severe MR or annular calcification, mitral repair or prosthesis, transplant, LVAD or constriction), each leading to its own advice. Step 1 chooses the algorithm. Algorithm 1 (normal LVEF, no myocardial disease) scores four criteria one by one: reduced e' (septal under 7 or lateral under 10 cm/s), average E/e' over 14, TR velocity over 2.8 m/s and LA volume index over 34 mL/m2; 0-1 abnormal is normal diastolic function, 2 is indeterminate, 3-4 is diastolic dysfunction, which continues to algorithm 2; a TR velocity or LA volume that cannot be obtained is skipped and the majority of the available criteria decides. Algorithm 2 uses the mitral inflow: E/A 2 or more is grade III with raised LA pressure; E/A 0.8 or less with E 50 cm/s or less is grade I with normal LA pressure; otherwise three criteria (E/e' over 14, TR velocity over 2.8 m/s, LA volume index over 34 mL/m2) decide: 2 or 3 positive is grade II with raised LA pressure, 2 or 3 negative is grade I with normal LA pressure, and only one criterion available, or two available that disagree, is indeterminate.
echo-diastolic-function-algorithm.attribution: Original decision tree for this study aid, based on the ASE/EACVI 2016 recommendations for the evaluation of left ventricular diastolic function.
echo-diastolic-function-algorithm.caption: Step through the ASE/EACVI 2016 approach: check the algorithms apply, then choose algorithm 1 (normal LVEF, no myocardial disease: is diastolic function normal?) or algorithm 2 (reduced LVEF or myocardial disease: grade I-III and LA pressure). Indeterminate results are reported as such. Superseded in part by the ASE 2025 diastolic function update (not yet reflected here). Study aid based on the cited guideline; verify against the current full guideline before clinical use.
echo-diastolic-function-algorithm.title: Diastolic function and filling pressure: ASE/EACVI 2016 algorithm

echo-hocm-dagger-cw.alt_text: Schematic continuous-wave Doppler spectrum from the apical five-chamber window with a reference ECG. The systolic signal below the baseline begins slowly with a concave upstroke, accelerates late and peaks sharply in late systole at 4.2 m/s, then falls abruptly at the end of ejection, giving a dagger-shaped (ski-slope) envelope. Footer: Vmax 4.2 m/s, peak gradient 4V squared = 71 mmHg. Finding: dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction as in hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, not fixed valvular aortic stenosis (whose envelope is rounded).
echo-hocm-dagger-cw.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
echo-hocm-dagger-cw.caption: Continuous-wave Doppler through the LVOT in obstructive HCM: the velocity builds slowly and peaks sharply in late systole ('dagger' or 'ski-slope' shape) as systolic anterior motion narrows the outflow during ejection. Vmax 4.2 m/s, peak gradient 71 mmHg (obstruction is a gradient of at least 30 mmHg; at least 50 mmHg is the threshold for septal reduction in symptomatic patients). Contrast the rounded envelope of valvular stenosis. Schematic, not a real recording.
echo-hocm-dagger-cw.title: CW Doppler: dynamic LVOT obstruction in HCM (late-peaking 'dagger', 4.2 m/s)

echo-lvot-pw-vti.alt_text: Schematic pulsed-wave Doppler with the sample volume in the LVOT (apical five-chamber view) and a reference ECG. Systolic flow lies below the baseline as a narrow band with a hollow centre (the clear spectral window of laminar flow), peaking early at about 1.1 m/s. The area under one envelope is shaded and labelled VTI 20 cm. Footer: VTI 20 cm, Vmax 1.1 m/s, SV = pi x (LVOT diameter / 2) squared x VTI. Finding: normal LVOT velocity-time integral (normal stroke volume).
echo-lvot-pw-vti.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
echo-lvot-pw-vti.caption: Pulsed-wave Doppler in the LVOT from the apical five-chamber view with the velocity-time integral shaded: stroke volume = LVOT area x LVOT VTI. VTI 20 cm is normal; with an LVOT diameter of 2.0 cm (area 3.14 cm2) the stroke volume is about 63 mL. Schematic, not a real recording.
echo-lvot-pw-vti.title: LVOT pulsed-wave Doppler with the VTI traced (20 cm)

echo-mitral-inflow-impaired-relaxation.alt_text: Schematic pulsed-wave Doppler of mitral inflow at the leaflet tips (apical four-chamber view), heart rate 60 per minute, with a reference ECG. A small E wave of 0.45 m/s decelerates slowly towards the baseline and is followed by a taller A wave of 0.75 m/s after the P wave. The long deceleration time is marked. Footer: E 0.45 m/s, A 0.75 m/s, E/A 0.6, DT 260 ms, IVRT 110 ms; septal e' 6 cm/s, E/e' 8. Finding: impaired relaxation (grade I diastolic dysfunction) with normal left atrial pressure.
echo-mitral-inflow-impaired-relaxation.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
echo-mitral-inflow-impaired-relaxation.caption: Grade I diastolic dysfunction (impaired relaxation, normal left atrial pressure): E smaller than A, prolonged deceleration time and IVRT, reduced e'. E/A of 0.8 or less with E of 50 cm/s or less means normal LA pressure (ASE/EACVI 2016). Schematic, not a real recording.
echo-mitral-inflow-impaired-relaxation.title: Mitral inflow: impaired relaxation, grade I (E/A 0.6, DT 260 ms)

echo-mitral-inflow-normal.alt_text: Schematic pulsed-wave Doppler of mitral inflow with the sample volume at the leaflet tips (apical four-chamber view), heart rate 60 per minute, with a reference ECG. Two diastolic waves lie above the baseline: an early E wave of 0.80 m/s after mitral opening that decelerates to the baseline, a pause (diastasis), and a smaller A wave of 0.55 m/s after the P wave. The deceleration slope is extended to the baseline and the deceleration time is marked. Footer: E 0.80 m/s, A 0.55 m/s, E/A 1.5, DT 200 ms, IVRT 80 ms; septal e' 10 cm/s, E/e' 8. Finding: normal LV filling.
echo-mitral-inflow-normal.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
echo-mitral-inflow-normal.caption: Pulsed-wave mitral inflow at the leaflet tips in a normal adult: E larger than A, deceleration time 160-200 ms, normal septal e' (10 cm/s) and E/e' 8. Schematic, not a real recording.
echo-mitral-inflow-normal.title: Mitral inflow: normal pattern (E/A 1.5, DT 200 ms, septal e' 10 cm/s)

echo-mitral-inflow-pseudonormal.alt_text: Schematic pulsed-wave Doppler of mitral inflow at the leaflet tips (apical four-chamber view), heart rate 60 per minute, with a reference ECG. The pattern resembles normal: an E wave of 0.85 m/s larger than an A wave of 0.60 m/s, but with a slightly shorter deceleration time. Footer: E 0.85 m/s, A 0.60 m/s, E/A 1.4, DT 170 ms, IVRT 75 ms; septal e' 5 cm/s (reduced), E/e' 17 (raised). Finding: pseudonormal filling, grade II diastolic dysfunction with raised left atrial pressure.
echo-mitral-inflow-pseudonormal.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
echo-mitral-inflow-pseudonormal.caption: Grade II diastolic dysfunction (pseudonormal filling): the inflow looks normal (E larger than A) because a raised left atrial pressure restores the early gradient, but the low e' (5 cm/s) and high E/e' (17) unmask it. Schematic, not a real recording.
echo-mitral-inflow-pseudonormal.title: Mitral inflow: pseudonormal, grade II (E/A 1.4, DT 170 ms, septal e' 5 cm/s, E/e' 17)

echo-mitral-inflow-restrictive.alt_text: Schematic pulsed-wave Doppler of mitral inflow at the leaflet tips (apical four-chamber view), heart rate 60 per minute, with a reference ECG. A tall, narrow E wave of 1.10 m/s decelerates very quickly to the baseline and is followed by a small A wave of 0.40 m/s. Footer: E 1.10 m/s, A 0.40 m/s, E/A 2.8, DT 130 ms, IVRT 50 ms; septal e' 4 cm/s, E/e' 28. Finding: restrictive filling, grade III diastolic dysfunction with markedly raised left atrial pressure.
echo-mitral-inflow-restrictive.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
echo-mitral-inflow-restrictive.caption: Grade III diastolic dysfunction (restrictive filling): a tall, narrow E wave with a very short deceleration time and a small A wave. An E/A of 2 or more means raised left atrial pressure (ASE/EACVI 2016). Schematic, not a real recording.
echo-mitral-inflow-restrictive.title: Mitral inflow: restrictive, grade III (E/A 2.8, DT 130 ms)

echo-mmode-mitral-epss.alt_text: Schematic M-mode through the mitral leaflet tips from the parasternal long-axis window with an ECG; depth in cm against time. From the top: the RV wall, the interventricular septum (a band with little systolic motion), the LV cavity, the anterior mitral leaflet (an M-shaped trace with E and A points marked) and the posterior leaflet (a mirror image in diastole; in systole the closed leaflets coapt into a single C-D line), and the LV posterior wall with little systolic thickening. A caliper marks the E-point septal separation between the E point and the septum: EPSS 15 mm. The leaflet opening is small and a shoulder (B-bump) interrupts the A-to-C closure. Footer: EPSS 15 mm, LVEDD 70 mm. Finding: dilated LV with severely reduced systolic function and raised end-diastolic pressure.
echo-mmode-mitral-epss.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
echo-mmode-mitral-epss.caption: M-mode through the mitral leaflet tips in a dilated, poorly contracting LV: the anterior leaflet's E point stays 15 mm from the septum (EPSS above about 7 mm suggests a reduced LVEF), the walls barely move, and a shoulder (B-bump) interrupts mitral closure, a sign of raised LV end-diastolic pressure. Schematic, not a real recording.
echo-mmode-mitral-epss.title: M-mode of the mitral valve: increased E-point septal separation (15 mm) in a dilated LV

echo-mmode-tapse.alt_text: Schematic M-mode through the lateral tricuspid annulus from the apical four-chamber view with an ECG; depth in cm with the transducer (apex) at the top. The bright annulus band moves towards the apex (upwards) in systole and back in diastole. Dashed lines at the end-diastolic and peak-systolic positions and an arrow between them measure the excursion: TAPSE 14 mm. Finding: reduced RV longitudinal systolic function (TAPSE below 17 mm).
echo-mmode-tapse.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
echo-mmode-tapse.caption: M-mode of the lateral tricuspid annulus from the apical four-chamber view: TAPSE is the systolic excursion of the annulus towards the apex. 14 mm is reduced RV longitudinal function (abnormal below 17 mm, ASE/EACVI 2015). Schematic, not a real recording.
echo-mmode-tapse.title: M-mode of the lateral tricuspid annulus: TAPSE 14 mm (reduced)

echo-mr-cw-severe.alt_text: Schematic continuous-wave Doppler from the apical four-chamber window with a reference ECG. A dense, dark holosystolic jet below the baseline begins at mitral closure (before aortic opening) and lasts until mitral opening. The velocity rises steeply to a peak of 4.6 m/s early in systole and then falls progressively through late systole, so the envelope is asymmetric and triangular rather than a flat plateau: the V-wave cut-off sign of a large left atrial v wave. Footer: Vmax 4.6 m/s. Finding: severe mitral regurgitation.
echo-mr-cw-severe.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
echo-mr-cw-severe.caption: Continuous-wave Doppler of severe mitral regurgitation: a dense holosystolic jet whose velocity peaks early and then falls through late systole (a triangular contour, the 'V-wave cut-off' of a large left atrial v wave). A faint, parabolic jet suggests mild MR; a dense triangular one supports severe MR (ASE 2017). Schematic, not a real recording.
echo-mr-cw-severe.title: CW Doppler: severe mitral regurgitation (dense jet, early peak, V-wave cut-off)

echo-ms-pressure-half-time.alt_text: Schematic continuous-wave Doppler of mitral inflow from the apical four-chamber window with a reference ECG, heart rate 60 per minute. Diastolic flow lies above the baseline (towards the transducer). After mitral opening the velocity rises to a peak of about 1.9 m/s and then falls along a slow, straight slope that is still well above the baseline when atrial contraction adds an A wave at end-diastole; a dashed line extends the slope to the baseline (a long deceleration time). Calipers mark the pressure half-time, the time for the velocity to fall from Vpeak to Vpeak divided by the square root of 2: 220 ms. Footer: MVA = 220 / PHT = 220 / 220 = 1.0 cm2. Finding: severe mitral stenosis.
echo-ms-pressure-half-time.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
echo-ms-pressure-half-time.caption: Continuous-wave Doppler of mitral inflow in mitral stenosis: a high early velocity with a slow, straight deceleration that has not reached the baseline when atrial contraction adds the A wave. Pressure half-time 220 ms, so MVA = 220 / PHT = 1.0 cm2: severe (ACC/AHA 2020: severe at 1.5 cm2 or less, very severe at 1.0 cm2 or less). Schematic, not a real recording.
echo-ms-pressure-half-time.title: Mitral stenosis: pressure half-time 220 ms, MVA 1.0 cm2 (severe)

echo-plax-view.alt_text: Schematic parasternal long-axis echocardiographic view at end-diastole, transducer at the top of the sector. From near to far: the RV free wall and RV outflow tract; the interventricular septum, continuous with the anterior wall of the aortic root; the LV cavity with the LVOT just below the septum; the open mitral valve, its anterior leaflet continuous with the posterior aortic wall and its posterior leaflet hinged at the atrioventricular groove; the aortic root on the right of the screen with the closed aortic valve (right coronary and non-coronary cusps); the left atrium behind the aortic root; the LV posterior wall with a papillary muscle; the pericardium; and the descending aorta in cross-section behind the left atrium. Normal anatomy.
echo-plax-view.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
echo-plax-view.caption: Parasternal long-axis view at end-diastole with the landmarks every PLAX question uses: the RV outflow nearest the transducer, the septum continuous with the anterior aortic wall, the anterior mitral leaflet continuous with the posterior aortic wall, and the descending aorta behind the left atrium (the landmark that separates pericardial from pleural fluid). Schematic, not a real recording.

echo-psax-aortic-level.alt_text: Schematic parasternal short-axis view at aortic valve level: the closed trileaflet aortic valve in the centre, its three commissure lines forming a Y (the 'Mercedes-Benz' sign), with the right coronary cusp anterior, the left coronary cusp to the right of the screen and the non-coronary cusp next to the interatrial septum. The RV outflow tract wraps around anteriorly from the tricuspid valve on the left to the pulmonary valve and main pulmonary artery on the right; the RA, the interatrial septum and the LA lie behind the aortic valve. Normal anatomy.
echo-psax-aortic-level.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
echo-psax-aortic-level.caption: Parasternal short-axis view at the aortic valve level: the closed trileaflet valve forms a Y ('Mercedes-Benz' sign), surrounded clockwise by the RA, RVOT, pulmonary valve and LA. The view for cusp number (bicuspid valve), the interatrial septum, the pulmonary valve and the tricuspid valve. Schematic, not a real recording.

echo-psax-mitral-level.alt_text: Schematic parasternal short-axis view at mitral valve level, viewed from the apex: a circular LV containing the fish-mouth mitral orifice open in diastole (anterior leaflet anterior, posterior leaflet posterior), with the crescent-shaped RV anterior and to the left of the screen. Dashed marks divide the LV wall into the six basal segments of the 17-segment model, labelled clockwise from the top: anterior, anterolateral, inferolateral, inferior, inferoseptal and anteroseptal. Normal anatomy.

echo-simpson-biplane-scheme.alt_text: Schematic of the biplane method of discs. The LV endocardium is traced in the apical four-chamber view (left) and the apical two-chamber view (right): solid outlines at end-diastole filled with 20 horizontal discs, and smaller dashed outlines at end-systole. The long axis L runs from the mitral annulus to the apex. Each disc is an ellipse with diameter a (in A4C) and b (in A2C), and the volume is V = pi/4 x sum of a x b x L/20. The figure states EDV 102 mL, ESV 42 mL and EF 59%, with EF = (EDV - ESV) / EDV: a normal ejection fraction.
echo-simpson-biplane-scheme.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
echo-simpson-biplane-scheme.caption: Biplane method of discs, the ASE/EACVI 2015 recommended 2-D method for LV volumes and LVEF: the endocardium is traced in A4C and A2C at end-diastole and end-systole and the cavity is summed as 20 elliptical discs. Here EDV 102 mL, ESV 42 mL, EF 59% (normal). Schematic, not a real recording.

echo-tamponade-respiratory-variation.alt_text: Schematic pulsed-wave Doppler of mitral inflow (upper panel) and tricuspid inflow (lower panel) at a heart rate of 80 per minute, with a respiratory trace and an ECG; inspiration is shaded. Mitral E falls from about 0.75 m/s in expiration to about 0.49 m/s at peak inspiration (about 35% lower), while tricuspid E rises reciprocally from about 0.45 m/s to 0.74 m/s (about 65% higher); the A waves stay constant. Finding: exaggerated reciprocal respiratory variation of inflow, as in cardiac tamponade.
echo-tamponade-respiratory-variation.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
echo-tamponade-respiratory-variation.caption: Mitral and tricuspid inflow recorded with respiration in cardiac tamponade: with inspiration mitral E falls by about 35% while tricuspid E rises by about 65% (exaggerated ventricular interdependence, the Doppler counterpart of pulsus paradoxus). Schematic, not a real recording.
echo-tamponade-respiratory-variation.title: Pulsed-wave Doppler: exaggerated reciprocal respiratory variation of mitral and tricuspid inflow (tamponade)

echo-tissue-doppler-septal.alt_text: Schematic pulsed-wave tissue Doppler at the septal mitral annulus (apical four-chamber view), velocities in cm/s, heart rate 60 per minute, with a reference ECG. Each cycle shows a brief isovolumic spike, the positive systolic s' wave (8 cm/s, motion towards the apex), a small isovolumic relaxation notch, and then two negative diastolic waves: early e' (10 cm/s) and, after the P wave, late a' (7 cm/s). Footer: s' 8 cm/s, e' 10 cm/s, a' 7 cm/s. Finding: normal septal annular velocities (e' at least 7 cm/s and larger than a').
echo-tissue-doppler-septal.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
echo-tissue-doppler-septal.caption: Pulsed-wave tissue Doppler of the septal mitral annulus: the systolic s' wave towards the apex and the early (e') and late (a') diastolic waves away from it. Septal e' 10 cm/s is normal (abnormal below 7 cm/s septal, below 10 cm/s lateral; ASE/EACVI 2016). Schematic, not a real recording.
echo-tissue-doppler-septal.title: Tissue Doppler of the septal mitral annulus: s', e' and a' (normal)

echo-tr-cw-pulmonary-hypertension.alt_text: Schematic continuous-wave Doppler from an RV-focused apical four-chamber view with a reference ECG. A holosystolic jet below the baseline with a steep onset, a flat rounded plateau and a steep end peaks at 3.6 m/s (dashed line). Footer: Vmax 3.6 m/s, peak gradient 4V squared = 52 mmHg. Adding an estimated right atrial pressure (for example 8 mmHg from the IVC) gives an RV systolic pressure of about 60 mmHg. Finding: TR peak velocity above 3.4 m/s, a high echocardiographic probability of pulmonary hypertension.
echo-tr-cw-pulmonary-hypertension.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
echo-tr-cw-pulmonary-hypertension.caption: Continuous-wave Doppler of tricuspid regurgitation: RVSP = 4V2 + RAP. A peak velocity of 3.6 m/s gives a gradient of 52 mmHg (RVSP about 60 mmHg with an RAP of 8 mmHg). A TR velocity above 3.4 m/s is a high echocardiographic probability of pulmonary hypertension (ESC/ERS 2022). Schematic, not a real recording.
echo-tr-cw-pulmonary-hypertension.title: CW Doppler: tricuspid regurgitation jet 3.6 m/s (estimated RVSP about 60 mmHg)

exercise-responses.alt_text: Six small line charts sharing a horizontal axis from rest to maximal workload. Heart rate rises in a straight line from about 70 to about 190 beats per minute. Stroke volume rises from about 70 mL to about 100 mL by mid-workload and then plateaus near 105 mL, with the plateau zone marked at 40 to 60 percent. Cardiac output rises from about 5 to about 20 L per minute. Blood pressure: systolic rises from about 120 to about 190 mmHg while diastolic stays near 80 and falls slightly. Systemic vascular resistance falls steeply from its resting value. The arteriovenous oxygen difference widens from about 5 to about 15 mL per dL. A vertical cursor moves across all six charts together; with reduced motion it is hidden and the charts are unchanged.
exercise-responses.attribution: Original schematic with illustrative values, after Guyton & Hall and Berne & Levy.
exercise-responses.caption: From rest to maximal dynamic exercise: HR rises linearly, SV plateaus at about 40-60% of VO2max, CO rises about four-fold, SBP rises while DBP barely changes, SVR falls and the a-vO2 difference widens. A cursor sweeps the workload axis.

fetal-circulation.alt_text: Schematic of the fetal circulation. Oxygenated blood leaves the placenta in the umbilical vein at about 80 to 85 percent saturation, bypasses the liver through the ductus venosus and enters the inferior vena cava at about 70 percent. In the right atrium this stream crosses the foramen ovale to the left atrium and left ventricle and leaves in the ascending aorta at about 65 percent, supplying the coronary arteries and brain. Desaturated superior vena cava blood at about 40 percent passes to the right ventricle and pulmonary artery at about 55 percent; because pulmonary vascular resistance is high, little enters the lungs and most crosses the ductus arteriosus right to left into the descending aorta at about 55 to 60 percent, which returns blood to the placenta through the umbilical arteries. Animated dots trace the two streams.
fetal-circulation.attribution: Original schematic with approximate saturations, after Rudolph, Guyton & Hall and Moss & Adams.
fetal-circulation.caption: Oxygenated umbilical-vein blood streams through the ductus venosus and foramen ovale to the LV, coronaries and brain; desaturated SVC blood goes to the RV and, because PVR is high, mostly crosses the ductus arteriosus to the descending aorta. Values are approximate.

fick-vo2.alt_text: A table-like diagram of the Fick equation: heart rate times stroke volume equals cardiac output, times arteriovenous oxygen difference equals oxygen uptake. Rest row: 70 per minute times 70 mL equals 4.9 L per minute, times 50 mL oxygen per litre equals about 250 mL per minute. Peak row: 190 times 105 mL equals about 20 L per minute, times 150 mL per litre equals about 3000 mL per minute. Fold-change row: heart rate 2.7 times, stroke volume 1.5 times, cardiac output 4 times, oxygen difference 3 times, oxygen uptake 12 times. Footnotes: rest is about 3.3 mL per kg per minute or 1 MET and peak about 40 mL per kg per minute or 11 METs for a 75 kg untrained adult; training raises maximal stroke volume and oxygen extraction, while maximal heart rate is fixed by age.
fick-vo2.attribution: Original schematic with illustrative values, after Guyton & Hall.
fick-vo2.caption: VO2 = HR x SV x (a-vO2 difference). From rest to peak, a twelve-fold rise in oxygen uptake comes from about four-fold more cardiac output and three-fold more extraction.

frank-starling.alt_text: A Frank-Starling curve plotting stroke volume or cardiac output against LV end-diastolic pressure (preload): the output rises steeply then plateaus. A moving operating point slides along the normal curve between lower and higher filling pressures. A dashed curve above shows increased contractility (shifted up and left) and a dotted curve below shows heart failure (shifted down and flattened). An inset of a sarcomere shows actin thin filaments overlapping a central myosin thick filament at the optimal length of about 2.2 micrometres, where increased length raises calcium sensitivity and force.
frank-starling.attribution: Original schematic, after Guyton & Hall and Pappano & Wiener.
frank-starling.caption: More end-diastolic stretch gives more stroke volume, up to a plateau. Increased contractility shifts the curve up and left; failure shifts it down. Inset: sarcomere length-tension.

gradient-flow-curves.alt_text: Curves of mean transaortic gradient against mean systolic flow rate for valve areas of 0.6, 0.8, 1.0 and 1.5 square centimetres, from the Gorlin relation: the gradient rises with the square of flow divided by area. A dashed line marks a mean gradient of 40 mmHg. A shaded low-flow zone on the left shows that a valve of 0.8 square centimetres produces a gradient well below 40 mmHg when flow is low, the low-flow low-gradient pattern, but more than 40 mmHg at normal flow.
gradient-flow-curves.attribution: Original schematic computed from the Gorlin relation, after Braunwald's Heart Disease.
gradient-flow-curves.caption: For a fixed valve area the mean gradient rises with the square of flow. A 0.8 cm² valve gives a low gradient at low flow and a severe-range gradient at normal flow: the basis of low-flow, low-gradient AS.
gradient-flow-curves.title: Gradient depends on flow

heart-failure-congestion.alt_text: Two vertical flow chains. Left-sided failure: LV systolic or diastolic failure, then raised LVEDP and left atrial pressure, then raised pulmonary capillary pressure (PCWP), then fluid into the lung interstitium and alveoli, ending in dyspnoea, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea and crackles. A dashed arrow labelled pulmonary hypertension links the left chain to the right chain. Right-sided failure: RV failure, most often from left heart failure, then raised RV filling and right atrial pressure, then raised systemic venous pressure (JVP), then fluid into the legs, sacrum, liver and gut, ending in oedema, hepatomegaly and ascites. A banner below states that in both, low effective arterial volume activates RAAS, the sympathetic system and ADH, causing sodium and water retention.
heart-failure-congestion.attribution: Original schematic, after Braunwald's Heart Disease.
heart-failure-congestion.caption: Left-sided failure congests the lungs; right-sided failure (most often caused by left-sided failure) congests the systemic veins. In both, neurohormonal activation makes the kidney retain Na+ and water.
heart-failure-congestion.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 360" role="img" aria-label="Congestion in left- versus right-sided heart failure" style="color:var(--ink)"><title>Left versus right heart failure congestion</title><desc>Two chains. Left-sided failure raises LV filling pressure and left atrial pressure, then pulmonary capillary pressure, so fluid enters the lung interstitium and alveoli, causing dyspnoea, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea and crackles. Right-sided failure, most often caused by left-sided failure through pulmonary hypertension, raises right atrial and systemic venous pressure, so fluid collects in the legs, liver and abdomen with a raised JVP, hepatomegaly and ascites. heart-sounds-timing.alt_text: Pressure curves for one cardiac cycle with grid lines at 0, 40, 80 and 120 mmHg: left ventricular pressure (solid), aortic pressure (dashed) and left atrial pressure (blue). Dashed vertical lines mark mitral closure (MC), aortic opening (AO), aortic closure (AC) and mitral opening (MO). Below, a sounds row: S4 just before S1 during atrial contraction; S1 at mitral closure with M1 then T1; an ejection click just after aortic opening; S2 at aortic closure with A2 then P2; an opening snap shortly after mitral opening (mitral stenosis); and S3 at the end of rapid filling. Notes below explain the mechanism of each sound.

ef.hint: ESC 2026 HF uses only two phenotypes: HFrEF = LVEF <50%, HFpEF = LVEF >=50% (HFmrEF removed). Exams may still use the 2021 universal definition categories.
