pe-murmur-areas-map.title: Auscultation areas of the anterior chest

aortic-features.hint: Feel the carotid upstroke and listen to A2: they tell you severity better than the loudness of the murmur.

options.label: Slow-rising small pulse, soft or absent A2, late-peaking murmur
Ejection click after S1, normal A2, mid-peaking murmur, young patient
Normal brisk carotid, normal A2, early-peaking soft murmur, elderly
Bounding pulse, wide pulse pressure, early diastolic murmur as well

aortic-features.text: Step 4 - Aortic outflow murmur. What accompanies it?

ar-setting.hint: Peripheral signs need a large stroke volume and time: they are florid in chronic AR and often absent in acute AR.

options.label: Gradual; wide pulse pressure, collapsing pulse, displaced apex, eponymous signs
Sudden dyspnoea or shock, short soft murmur, soft S1, little pulse widening
Fever, embolic phenomena, new or changing murmur

ar-setting.text: Step 4 - Aortic regurgitation. How did it present and what do the pulses show?

cont.hint: A continuous murmur needs a pressure difference throughout the cycle (aorta to pulmonary artery, artery to vein).

options.label: Left infraclavicular area, machinery quality, peaks at S2
Right supraclavicular fossa, disappears lying flat or with light jugular pressure
Unusual site (precordium, back, limb) or sudden onset with chest pain

cont.text: Step 3 - Continuous murmur. Where is it maximal and how does it behave?

dia-shape.hint: Every diastolic murmur is pathological. Use the diaphragm for high-pitched early diastolic murmurs and the bell for low-pitched rumbles.

options.label: Immediately after S2: high-pitched, blowing, decrescendo (early diastolic)
After a gap or an opening snap: low-pitched rumble (mid-diastolic, with or without presystolic accentuation)

dia-shape.text: Step 2 - Shape (diastolic). When does it start and what is its pitch?

early-dia.hint: Sit the patient forward, ask for a breath out and hold; listen at the left sternal edge with the diaphragm.

options.label: Left sternal border, 3rd-4th intercostal space (Erb's point)
Right sternal border more than left
Left upper sternal border, louder on inspiration, loud P2, RV heave
Left upper sternal border, low-pitched, starts after a gap from P2, after tetralogy repair or pulmonary valvotomy

early-dia.text: Step 3 - Site (early diastolic murmur). Where is it loudest?

early-sys.hint: An early systolic, decrescendo murmur means the pressure difference driving the leak disappears before the end of systole.

options.label: Child or young adult, well, localised murmur at the left sternal border
Sudden pulmonary oedema or shock, soft murmur, large v waves
Left lower sternal border, louder on inspiration, normal RV pressure

early-sys.text: Step 4 - Early systolic murmur. What is the setting?

ejection-site.hint: Grade it too (Levine 1-6; a thrill means grade 4 or more).

options.label: Right 2nd intercostal space, radiates to both carotids
Left lower sternal border/apex, no carotid radiation, harsh
Soft (grade 1-2), short, early-peaking, normal S2, otherwise normal heart

ejection-site.text: Step 3 - Site and radiation (ejection murmur). Where is it loudest and where does it go?

hcm-test.hint: Valsalva strain and standing reduce preload (smaller LV); squatting and passive leg raise increase it.

options.label: Louder with Valsalva/standing, softer with squatting and handgrip
Softer with Valsalva/standing, louder with squatting, slow-rising pulse or soft A2 (AS heard at the apex)
Softer with Valsalva/standing, normal pulse and S2, in fever, anaemia, pregnancy or thyrotoxicosis
Soft (grade 1-2), vibratory, child or young adult, otherwise normal heart

hcm-test.text: Step 4 - Dynamic test. What happens with Valsalva strain or on standing from squatting?

holo-site.hint: Carvallo sign: a right-sided holosystolic murmur increases during inspiration.

options.label: Apex, radiating to the left axilla, no change with respiration
Left lower sternal border, louder on inspiration, large cv waves in the neck
Left lower sternal border (3rd-4th space), harsh, with a thrill, no change with respiration

holo-site.text: Step 3 - Site, radiation and respiration (holosystolic murmur). Where is it loudest?

late-sys.hint: Anything that makes the LV smaller (standing, Valsalva) brings prolapse earlier.

options.label: Mid-systolic click; click and murmur move earlier and the murmur gets longer on standing/Valsalva
No click; in a patient with ischaemic heart disease, varies with ischaemia

late-sys.text: Step 4 - Late systolic murmur. Is there a click, and how does it move with posture?

mid-dia.hint: Listen at the apex with the bell, patient turned to the left lateral position, ideally after a little exercise.

options.label: Apex: loud S1, opening snap, presystolic accentuation in sinus rhythm
Apex: severe AR present, no opening snap, S1 normal or soft
Apex or left sternal border with S3: large left-to-right shunt or severe MR
Varies with posture; early diastolic 'plop'; constitutional symptoms
Left lower sternal border, louder on inspiration, giant a waves
Left upper sternal border, short, after tetralogy repair or pulmonary valvotomy

mid-dia.text: Step 3 - Mid-diastolic rumble. Where is it, and what goes with it?

mr-features.hint: Handgrip (more afterload) makes MR louder; amyl nitrite makes it softer.

options.label: Soft S1, S3, displaced hyperdynamic apex, slow onset
Days after an MI, with sudden pulmonary oedema or shock
Fever, new murmur, splinter haemorrhages or emboli

mr-features.text: Step 4 - Apical holosystolic murmur. What is the setting?

pulm-site.hint: Listen at the left upper sternal border in both phases of respiration.

options.label: Wide split S2 that does not move with respiration (fixed)
Ejection click that gets softer on inspiration; long murmur, soft delayed P2
Normal splitting; soft murmur in fever, anaemia, pregnancy or thyrotoxicosis

pulm-site.text: Step 4 - Pulmonary-area ejection murmur. What do S2 and the click do?

r-ar-acute.cite: ESC/EACTS 2025 and ACC/AHA 2020 valvular heart disease guidelines; Braunwald's Heart Disease; ESC 2023 infective endocarditis guidelines
r-ar-acute.detail:
- Sudden pulmonary oedema and shock; tachycardia; the murmur is **short and soft** because LV and aortic diastolic pressures equalise early.
- **Soft S1** (early mitral closure), little or no widening of the pulse pressure, no peripheral signs.
- Urgent echo/CT; emergency surgery; avoid IABP (it worsens AR).
r-ar-acute.text: Acute severe aortic regurgitation (endocarditis, dissection): surgical emergency

r-ar-chronic.cite: ESC/EACTS 2025 and ACC/AHA 2020 valvular heart disease guidelines; Braunwald's Heart Disease
r-ar-chronic.detail:
- Early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal edge; the **longer** the murmur, the more severe (until very late disease).
- **Collapsing (water-hammer, Corrigan) pulse**, wide pulse pressure, displaced hyperdynamic apex; eponymous signs (de Musset, Quincke, Duroziez, Traube, Muller, Hill).
- An apical mid-diastolic rumble may be an Austin Flint murmur.
- Surgery when severe and symptomatic, or LVEF 50% or less, or LVESD over 50 mm (or 25 mm/m2) (ESC/EACTS; ACC/AHA 2020 uses LVEF 55% or less).

r-ar-root.cite: ESC/EACTS 2025 and ACC/AHA 2020 valvular heart disease guidelines; Braunwald's Heart Disease; ESC 2024 peripheral arterial and aortic diseases guidelines
r-ar-root.detail:
- An early diastolic murmur louder at the **right** sternal border suggests a dilated aortic root (Marfan, annuloaortic ectasia, syphilis) or **aortic dissection**.
- With chest/back pain, pulse or BP differences between arms, or a new murmur: emergency CT or TOE.
r-ar-root.text: Aortic regurgitation from aortic root disease: exclude dissection

r-as-bicuspid.cite: ESC/EACTS 2025 and ACC/AHA 2020 valvular heart disease guidelines; Braunwald's Heart Disease; ESC 2020 ACHD
r-as-bicuspid.detail:
- The **ejection click** after S1 means the leaflets are still mobile; it disappears as the valve calcifies.
- Mid-peaking murmur and preserved A2 suggest mild to moderate stenosis.
- Look for coarctation (radio-femoral delay, arm-leg BP difference) and image the aorta (aortopathy).
- First-degree relatives: screening echo is advised.
r-as-bicuspid.text: Bicuspid aortic valve with stenosis (mobile valve)

r-as-severe.cite: ESC/EACTS 2025 and ACC/AHA 2020 valvular heart disease guidelines; Braunwald's Heart Disease
r-as-severe.detail:
- Bedside markers of severity: **slow-rising, small carotid (parvus et tardus)**, **late-peaking** murmur, **soft or absent A2** (single S2 or paradoxical splitting), sustained apex, S4.
- Loudness is **not** a severity marker: with low flow (poor LV) the murmur can be soft.
- Gallavardin phenomenon: the high-frequency part can radiate to the apex and mimic MR.
- Symptoms (angina, syncope, dyspnoea) in severe AS = intervention (SAVR/TAVI by the Heart Team); asymptomatic severe high-gradient AS with LVEF 50% or more and low procedural risk: intervention should be considered (ESC/EACTS 2025, IIa).
r-as-severe.text: Severe aortic stenosis: confirm with echo (Vmax, mean gradient, AVA)

r-asd.cite: ESC 2020 adult congenital heart disease guidelines; Braunwald's Heart Disease
r-asd.detail:
- **Wide, fixed splitting of S2**, soft pulmonary ejection (flow) murmur, sometimes a tricuspid mid-diastolic flow rumble.
- RV heave; ECG: RBBB pattern with right axis deviation (left axis in primum ASD).
- Confirm with echo (TOE for anatomy); closure if there is right heart volume overload and no severe pulmonary vascular disease.

r-austin-flint.cite: ESC/EACTS 2025 and ACC/AHA 2020 valvular heart disease guidelines; Braunwald's Heart Disease
r-austin-flint.detail:
- Apical mid-to-late diastolic rumble in severe AR: the regurgitant jet hits the anterior mitral leaflet and partly closes it (functional MS).
- No opening snap, S1 not loud; **amyl nitrite softens it** (less AR) whereas it makes true MS louder.
- Treat as severe AR.
r-austin-flint.text: Austin Flint murmur of severe aortic regurgitation

r-fistula.cite: ESC 2020 adult congenital heart disease guidelines; Braunwald's Heart Disease
r-fistula.detail:
- Coronary artery fistula (lower precordium, peaks in diastole), systemic AV fistula (limb, dialysis access), pulmonary AV malformation.
- **Sudden** continuous murmur with chest pain and heart failure: **ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm** (into the RA or RV) - emergency echo.
- Echo, CT or catheter angiography to define the communication.
r-fistula.text: Other continuous murmurs: fistula or ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm

r-flow.cite: Braunwald's Heart Disease (physical examination); Bates' Guide to Physical Examination
r-flow.detail:
- Increased flow across a normal pulmonary or aortic valve: fever, anaemia, pregnancy, thyrotoxicosis, AV fistula.
- Soft, early-peaking, normal S2; disappears when the cause is treated.
- Treat the cause; echo if any atypical feature.
r-flow.text: Flow murmur from a high-output state

r-flow-rumble.cite: Braunwald's Heart Disease (physical examination); Bates' Guide to Physical Examination
r-flow-rumble.detail:
- High flow across the mitral valve (severe MR, large VSD or PDA) or the tricuspid valve (large ASD): short mid-diastolic rumble, usually with an S3.
- Indicates a large shunt (Qp/Qs about 2 or more) or severe regurgitation.
- Carey Coombs murmur: soft mid-diastolic murmur in acute rheumatic carditis (valvulitis).
r-flow-rumble.text: Diastolic flow rumble across a normal AV valve

r-graham-steell.cite: ESC/EACTS 2025 and ACC/AHA 2020 valvular heart disease guidelines; Braunwald's Heart Disease; ESC/ERS 2022 pulmonary hypertension guidelines
r-graham-steell.detail:
- High-pitched early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left upper sternal border, **louder on inspiration**, with a **loud P2**, RV heave, raised JVP.
- Classically in MS with severe pulmonary hypertension; distinguish from AR (peripheral signs, no inspiratory increase).
- Echo: estimate PA pressures and look for the cause.
r-graham-steell.text: Pulmonary regurgitation from pulmonary hypertension (Graham Steell murmur)

r-hcm.cite: ESC 2023 cardiomyopathy guidelines; AHA/ACC 2024 HCM guideline
r-hcm.detail:
- Harsh mid-systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border/apex, **no carotid radiation**, **jerky (spike-and-dome) pulse**, double or triple apical impulse, S4.
- **Louder** with Valsalva strain and standing (less preload); **softer** with squatting, passive leg raise and handgrip.
- Often accompanied by MR (systolic anterior motion of the mitral leaflet).
- Echo: wall thickness 15 mm or more, LVOT gradient (30 mmHg or more at rest or on provocation = obstruction; 50 mmHg or more = haemodynamically important, the threshold for septal reduction therapy when symptoms persist on optimal medical therapy); avoid vasodilators and dehydration; screen relatives.
r-hcm.text: Dynamic LVOT obstruction: obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

r-ie.detail:
- New or changing regurgitant murmur with fever.
- Look for **splinter haemorrhages, Janeway lesions** (painless, palms and soles), **Osler nodes** (painful, finger pulps), **Roth spots** (retinal), clubbing, splenomegaly, haematuria, emboli.
- Three sets of blood cultures before antibiotics; TTE then TOE; modified Duke criteria (ESC 2023); early surgery for heart failure, uncontrolled infection or embolic risk.
r-ie.text: Suspect infective endocarditis: blood cultures before antibiotics, then echo

r-innocent.cite: Braunwald's Heart Disease (physical examination); Bates' Guide to Physical Examination
r-innocent.detail:
- Features: grade 1-2, short, early-to-mid systolic, ejection, normal S1 and S2 (normal splitting), no click, no thrill, normal pulses and apex, no symptoms.
- Varieties: Still's murmur (vibratory, children), pulmonary flow murmur, supraclavicular arterial bruit. Aortic sclerosis is not an innocent murmur (see the aortic outflow branch).
- Any diastolic murmur, a grade 3 or louder murmur, a thrill, an abnormal S2, symptoms or an abnormal ECG means **echocardiography**.
r-innocent.text: Innocent (functional) systolic murmur likely: confirm the whole examination is normal

r-mixed-aortic.cite: ESC/EACTS 2025 and ACC/AHA 2020 valvular heart disease guidelines; Braunwald's Heart Disease
r-mixed-aortic.detail:
- Ejection systolic murmur (increased stroke volume, with or without stenosis) plus an early diastolic murmur: a **to-and-fro** murmur, not a continuous one.
- Pulsus **bisferiens** is classic when both lesions are significant (or in severe AR alone).
- Severity of each lesion is graded by echo; the dominant lesion guides timing of surgery.
r-mixed-aortic.text: Mixed aortic valve disease (stenosis and regurgitation)

r-mr-acute.cite: ESC/EACTS 2025 and ACC/AHA 2020 valvular heart disease guidelines; Braunwald's Heart Disease; ACC/AHA 2025 ACS guideline
r-mr-acute.detail:
- After MI (often inferior, posteromedial papillary muscle) or with endocarditis or chordal rupture: sudden pulmonary oedema, hypotension.
- The murmur is often **soft, short, early systolic and decrescendo** (the small non-compliant LA quickly equalises with the LV: large v wave), so it can be missed.
- Urgent echo; afterload reduction and IABP/mechanical support as a bridge; emergency surgery.
r-mr-acute.text: Acute severe mitral regurgitation (papillary muscle rupture, chordal rupture, endocarditis): emergency

r-mr-chronic.cite: ESC/EACTS 2025 and ACC/AHA 2020 valvular heart disease guidelines; Braunwald's Heart Disease
r-mr-chronic.detail:
- Soft S1, holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, **S3** (volume load, not necessarily failure), displaced hyperdynamic apex.
- Primary (degenerative/prolapse, rheumatic) or secondary (dilated LV, ischaemic).
- Echo: EROA, regurgitant volume, LV size and function; surgery when severe and symptomatic or with LV dysfunction (LVEF 60% or less, LVESD 40 mm or more, or LVESD indexed 20 mm/m2 or more).

r-ms.cite: ESC/EACTS 2025 and ACC/AHA 2020 valvular heart disease guidelines; Braunwald's Heart Disease
r-ms.detail:
- Loud S1 (mobile leaflets), **opening snap**, low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble at the apex in the left lateral position with **presystolic accentuation** in sinus rhythm (lost in AF).
- The **shorter the A2-OS interval** and the **longer the rumble**, the more severe the stenosis.
- Malar flush, AF, signs of pulmonary hypertension (loud P2, Graham Steell murmur).
- Echo: valve area (severe 1.5 cm2 or less), Wilkins score; PMC for suitable valves; anticoagulation with AF (VKA in moderate-severe MS).

r-mvp.cite: ESC/EACTS 2025 and ACC/AHA 2020 valvular heart disease guidelines; Braunwald's Heart Disease
r-mvp.detail:
- **Mid-systolic click** followed by a **late systolic murmur** at the apex.
- Standing and Valsalva (smaller LV) make the click come **earlier** and the murmur **longer**; squatting and handgrip delay the click and shorten the murmur.
- Echo: leaflet displacement over 2 mm beyond the annulus in the parasternal long-axis view; follow the degree of MR.

r-myxoma.cite: Braunwald's Heart Disease (physical examination); Bates' Guide to Physical Examination
r-myxoma.detail:
- Mid-diastolic murmur that changes with posture, early diastolic **tumour plop**, syncope, emboli, fever, weight loss, raised ESR.
- Echo diagnosis; urgent surgical excision (embolic risk).

r-papillary.cite: ESC/EACTS 2025 and ACC/AHA 2020 valvular heart disease guidelines; Braunwald's Heart Disease
r-papillary.detail:
- Late systolic or variable apical murmur that comes and goes with ischaemia.
- Treat the ischaemia; assess MR severity on echo at rest and, if needed, with stress.

r-pda.cite: ESC 2020 adult congenital heart disease guidelines; Braunwald's Heart Disease
r-pda.detail:
- Continuous **machinery (Gibson) murmur** at the left infraclavicular area, peaking around S2, with a collapsing pulse when the shunt is large.
- With Eisenmenger physiology the murmur disappears and **differential cyanosis** appears (feet blue and clubbed, hands pink).
- Echo; transcatheter closure for a significant shunt without severe pulmonary vascular disease.

r-pr-low.cite: ESC 2020 adult congenital heart disease guidelines; Braunwald's Heart Disease
r-pr-low.detail:
- Low-pitched, short, crescendo-decrescendo early-to-mid diastolic murmur starting after P2, louder on inspiration.
- Typical after tetralogy repair or pulmonary valvotomy; follow RV size on CMR.

r-ps.cite: ESC 2020 adult congenital heart disease guidelines; Braunwald's Heart Disease
r-ps.detail:
- Ejection click that **softens on inspiration** (the only right-sided event that does), ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border.
- The more severe the stenosis: the **longer** the murmur, the **closer** the click to S1, the **later and softer** P2 (wide split), RV heave, prominent a wave.
- Echo for the gradient; balloon valvuloplasty for significant stenosis.

r-rub.cite: ESC 2025 myocarditis and pericarditis guidelines; Braunwald's Heart Disease
r-rub.detail:
- Scratchy, superficial, high-pitched; up to **three components** (atrial systole, ventricular systole, early diastolic filling); best at the left sternal border with the patient sitting forward in held expiration; varies from hour to hour.
- With pleuritic chest pain and widespread concave ST elevation: acute pericarditis (NSAID + colchicine).
- Watch for tamponade (rising JVP, falling BP, pulsus paradoxus).

r-sclerosis.cite: ESC/EACTS 2025 and ACC/AHA 2020 valvular heart disease guidelines; Braunwald's Heart Disease
r-sclerosis.detail:
- Elderly, soft early-peaking ejection murmur, **normal carotid upstroke and normal A2**.
- Thickened leaflets without obstruction (Vmax under 2.5 m/s on echo).
- A marker of cardiovascular risk; follow clinically.
r-sclerosis.text: Aortic sclerosis (no outflow obstruction) likely; echo to exclude stenosis

r-small-vsd.cite: ESC 2020 adult congenital heart disease guidelines; Braunwald's Heart Disease
r-small-vsd.detail:
- The murmur stops when the contracting muscle closes the defect in late systole, so it is early systolic and localised.
- Many close spontaneously; endocarditis prophylaxis by hygiene; follow-up echo.
r-small-vsd.text: Small muscular VSD: early systolic murmur

r-tr.cite: ESC/EACTS 2025 and ACC/AHA 2020 valvular heart disease guidelines; Braunwald's Heart Disease
r-tr.detail:
- Holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that **increases on inspiration (Carvallo sign)**.
- Raised JVP with **giant cv waves** (lost x descent), pulsatile liver, RV heave, peripheral oedema.
- Usually secondary (functional: RV dilatation from left heart disease, pulmonary hypertension, AF); primary causes include endocarditis (IV drug use), carcinoid, Ebstein anomaly, pacing leads.

r-ts.cite: ESC/EACTS 2025 and ACC/AHA 2020 valvular heart disease guidelines; Braunwald's Heart Disease
r-ts.detail:
- Mid-diastolic rumble at the left lower sternal border, **louder on inspiration**, with giant a waves and a slow y descent in the JVP.
- Rheumatic (almost always with mitral disease) or carcinoid.

r-venous-hum.cite: Braunwald's Heart Disease (physical examination); Bates' Guide to Physical Examination
r-venous-hum.detail:
- Continuous hum above the right clavicle in children and in high-output states, loudest sitting, **abolished by lying flat, turning the head towards the side of the hum, or light pressure on the internal jugular vein** (turning away accentuates it).
- The only common innocent continuous murmur (with the mammary souffle of pregnancy).

r-vsd.cite: ESC 2020 adult congenital heart disease guidelines; Braunwald's Heart Disease; ACC/AHA 2025 ACS guideline
r-vsd.detail:
- Loud, harsh holosystolic murmur at the left 3rd-4th intercostal space with a **thrill**; loudness reflects the pressure gradient, so a small defect can be very loud (maladie de Roger).
- Large defects with pulmonary hypertension: the murmur shortens and softens (Eisenmenger: murmur may disappear, loud P2, cyanosis).
- **New harsh murmur with a thrill 3-5 days after MI** = post-infarction VSD: emergency (shock), surgical or transcatheter repair.

sys-shape.hint: Ejection murmurs start after S1 (isovolumic contraction is silent) and stop before the S2 of their side; regurgitant murmurs start with S1.

options.label: Ejection: crescendo-decrescendo, starts after S1, ends before S2
Holosystolic (pansystolic): plateau from S1 up to S2
Late systolic: starts in mid-systole, often after a click
Early systolic only: decrescendo, ends in mid-systole

sys-shape.text: Step 2 - Shape (systolic). What is its shape and length?

timing.hint: S1 coincides with the carotid upstroke; systole (S1 to S2) is shorter than diastole at normal heart rates. Palpate the carotid while you listen.

options.label: Diastolic: between S2 and the next S1
Continuous: starts in systole and runs through S2 into diastole
Separate systolic and diastolic components, a gap at S2 (to-and-fro)

timing.text: Step 1 - Timing. When does the murmur occur? Time it against S1, S2 and the carotid upstroke.

tofro.hint: A to-and-fro murmur (systolic + diastolic with a break at S2) is not a continuous murmur.

options.label: Scratchy, superficial, up to three components, changes with position
Ejection systolic + early diastolic murmur at the aortic area

tofro.text: Step 2 - Two components. What do they sound like?

pe-murmur-identification-algorithm.alt_text: Decision tree for identifying a heart murmur. Step 1 times it: systolic, diastolic, continuous, or to-and-fro. Systolic murmurs split by shape: ejection (crescendo-decrescendo) murmurs by site into aortic outflow (severe calcific stenosis with a slow-rising pulse and soft A2, bicuspid valve with an ejection click, aortic sclerosis, mixed aortic disease), obstructive HCM (louder with Valsalva and standing, softer with squatting; a non-dynamic murmur there exits to aortic stenosis, a flow murmur or an innocent murmur), pulmonary-area murmurs (atrial septal defect with wide fixed splitting, pulmonary stenosis with a click that softens on inspiration, flow murmurs) and innocent murmurs; holosystolic murmurs into mitral regurgitation (chronic, acute after MI, endocarditis), tricuspid regurgitation (Carvallo sign) and VSD; late systolic murmurs into mitral valve prolapse and papillary muscle dysfunction; early systolic murmurs into small VSD, acute MR and TR. Diastolic murmurs split into early diastolic (aortic regurgitation chronic or acute, aortic root disease, Graham Steell murmur, low-pressure pulmonary regurgitation after tetralogy repair) and mid-diastolic rumbles (mitral stenosis, Austin Flint, flow rumbles, myxoma, tricuspid stenosis). Continuous murmurs: PDA, venous hum, fistula or ruptured sinus of Valsalva. To-and-fro: pericardial rub or mixed aortic disease.
pe-murmur-identification-algorithm.attribution: Original decision tree for this study aid, based on Braunwald's Heart Disease and Bates' Guide to Physical Examination, and the ESC/EACTS 2025 and ACC/AHA 2020 valvular, ESC 2023 endocarditis, ESC 2023 cardiomyopathy and ESC 2020 adult congenital heart disease guidelines.
pe-murmur-identification-algorithm.caption: Work a murmur out in a fixed order: timing (systolic, diastolic, continuous, to-and-fro), shape, site and radiation, the effect of respiration and manoeuvres, then the accompanying signs that point to the lesion and its severity. Study aid based on the cited textbooks and guidelines; verify against the current full guideline before clinical use.
pe-murmur-identification-algorithm.title: Murmur identification: timing, shape, site and radiation, manoeuvres, likely lesion

pe-phono-aortic-regurgitation.alt_text: Schematic phonocardiogram under a reference ECG at 70 per minute, two cycles; S1 and S2 are labelled. Systole is clear between S1 and S2. Immediately after S2 a high-pitched murmur of closely spaced vibrations begins at its loudest and fades steadily (decrescendo) through the first half to two thirds of diastole, ending before the next S1. Early diastolic decrescendo murmur: aortic regurgitation (left sternal edge, patient sitting forward in held expiration, diaphragm).
pe-phono-aortic-regurgitation.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
pe-phono-aortic-regurgitation.caption: Aortic regurgitation: a high-pitched, blowing early diastolic decrescendo murmur starting immediately after A2. Schematic, not a real recording.
pe-phono-aortic-regurgitation.title: Aortic regurgitation: early diastolic decrescendo murmur

pe-phono-aortic-stenosis.alt_text: Schematic phonocardiogram (sound amplitude against time) under a reference ECG at 70 per minute, two cardiac cycles; S1 and S2 are labelled. In systole a diamond-shaped (crescendo-decrescendo) ejection murmur begins after S1, builds to a late peak (in the second half of systole) and ends just before S2. S2 is soft (diminished A2). There is no ejection click after S1 and diastole is silent. Late-peaking ejection systolic murmur with a soft A2: severe calcific aortic stenosis (heard at the right second intercostal space, radiating to the carotids).
pe-phono-aortic-stenosis.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
pe-phono-aortic-stenosis.caption: Severe calcific aortic stenosis: a crescendo-decrescendo (ejection) systolic murmur that starts after S1, peaks late and ends before a soft S2, with no ejection click (the calcified valve is immobile). Schematic, not a real recording.
pe-phono-aortic-stenosis.title: Severe calcific aortic stenosis: late-peaking ejection systolic murmur

pe-phono-aortic-stenosis-bicuspid-click.alt_text: Schematic phonocardiogram under a reference ECG at 70 per minute, two cycles; S1 and S2 are labelled. A short, sharp, high-pitched sound (the aortic ejection click, not labelled in the picture) follows S1 by about 50 ms, at the onset of ejection. A crescendo-decrescendo ejection murmur then peaks in mid-systole (earlier than in severe stenosis) and ends before a normal-intensity S2 (A2 preserved). Ejection click + mid-peaking ejection murmur: mobile bicuspid aortic valve with mild to moderate stenosis.
pe-phono-aortic-stenosis-bicuspid-click.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
pe-phono-aortic-stenosis-bicuspid-click.caption: Bicuspid aortic valve with stenosis: a sharp ejection click just after S1 (the mobile, doming valve), then a mid-peaking crescendo-decrescendo murmur and a preserved A2. Schematic, not a real recording.
pe-phono-aortic-stenosis-bicuspid-click.title: Bicuspid aortic valve: ejection click and ejection systolic murmur

pe-phono-hcm-valsalva.alt_text: Schematic phonocardiogram in two panels, Rest and Valsalva (strain), each with a reference ECG at 70 per minute; S1 and S2 are labelled. At rest a soft crescendo-decrescendo murmur sits in mid-systole between S1 and S2. During the strain phase of Valsalva the same murmur is more than twice as loud; S1 and S2 are unchanged. A systolic ejection murmur that increases with Valsalva (and on standing, decreasing on squatting or handgrip): dynamic LVOT obstruction of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (the murmur of aortic stenosis does the opposite).
pe-phono-hcm-valsalva.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
pe-phono-hcm-valsalva.caption: Obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: the mid-systolic ejection murmur at the left lower sternal border is soft at rest and becomes much louder in the strain phase of the Valsalva manoeuvre (less preload, more outflow obstruction). Schematic, not a real recording.
pe-phono-hcm-valsalva.title: Obstructive HCM murmur: louder with Valsalva

pe-phono-mitral-regurgitation.alt_text: Schematic phonocardiogram under a reference ECG at 70 per minute, two cycles; S1 and S2 are labelled. S1 is soft. A plateau-shaped (uniform intensity) murmur of closely packed, high-pitched vibrations starts with S1 and lasts the whole of systole, reaching S2. Diastole is silent. Holosystolic (pansystolic) murmur with a soft S1: chronic mitral regurgitation (apex, radiating to the axilla).
pe-phono-mitral-regurgitation.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
pe-phono-mitral-regurgitation.caption: Chronic mitral regurgitation: a soft S1 and a high-pitched holosystolic (pansystolic) plateau murmur running from S1 up to and through A2. Schematic, not a real recording.
pe-phono-mitral-regurgitation.title: Chronic mitral regurgitation: holosystolic murmur

pe-phono-mitral-stenosis.alt_text: Schematic phonocardiogram under a reference ECG at 70 per minute (sinus rhythm), two cycles; S1 and S2 are labelled. S1 is loud (the largest sound). About 80 ms after S2 comes a short, sharp sound (the opening snap, not labelled). From it a low-pitched, coarse, widely spaced murmur (rumble) starts, fades through mid-diastole, then rises again in late diastole after the P wave (presystolic accentuation) to merge into the loud S1. Systole is quiet. Loud S1 + opening snap + mid-diastolic rumble with presystolic accentuation: mitral stenosis (apex, left lateral position, bell).
pe-phono-mitral-stenosis.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
pe-phono-mitral-stenosis.caption: Rheumatic mitral stenosis in sinus rhythm: loud S1, an opening snap shortly after S2, then a low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble with presystolic accentuation into S1. Schematic, not a real recording.
pe-phono-mitral-stenosis.title: Mitral stenosis: loud S1, opening snap, rumble with presystolic accentuation

pe-phono-pda-continuous.alt_text: Schematic phonocardiogram under a reference ECG at 70 per minute, two cycles; S1 and S2 are labelled. A murmur begins shortly after S1, rises steadily through systole, is loudest around S2, which it envelops, and continues into diastole, fading towards the next S1, with only a short gap before S1. Continuous (machinery, Gibson) murmur peaking at S2: patent ductus arteriosus (left infraclavicular area).
pe-phono-pda-continuous.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
pe-phono-pda-continuous.caption: Patent ductus arteriosus: a continuous machinery murmur that builds through systole, peaks around S2 (which it envelops) and fades through diastole. Schematic, not a real recording.
pe-phono-pda-continuous.title: Patent ductus arteriosus: continuous machinery murmur

pe-phono-s3.alt_text: Schematic phonocardiogram under a reference ECG at 70 per minute, two cycles; S1 and S2 are labelled. Besides S1 and S2 there is a third, unlabelled, low-pitched (slow, dull) sound in early diastole about 150 ms after S2, with no murmur: the third heart sound (S3, protodiastolic or ventricular gallop). Normal in children, young adults, athletes and pregnancy; after about 40 years it signals volume overload or systolic heart failure (or severe MR).
pe-phono-s3.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
pe-phono-s3.caption: Third heart sound: a low-pitched early diastolic sound about 150 ms after S2, at the end of rapid ventricular filling (ventricular gallop). Schematic, not a real recording.
pe-phono-s3.title: Third heart sound (S3)

pe-phono-s4.alt_text: Schematic phonocardiogram under a reference ECG at 70 per minute, two cycles; S1 and S2 are labelled. A low-pitched (slow, dull) unlabelled sound occurs in late diastole after the P wave of the ECG and about 100 ms before S1, with no murmur: the fourth heart sound (S4, presystolic or atrial gallop). Caused by atrial contraction into a non-compliant ventricle (LVH, hypertension, aortic stenosis, HCM, acute ischaemia); it needs an atrial contraction, so it is absent in atrial fibrillation.
pe-phono-s4.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
pe-phono-s4.caption: Fourth heart sound: a low-pitched late diastolic (presystolic) sound just before S1, after the P wave, from atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle. Schematic, not a real recording.
pe-phono-s4.title: Fourth heart sound (S4)

pe-phono-split-s2-paradoxical.alt_text: Schematic phonocardiogram in two panels, Expiration and Inspiration, each under a reference ECG with a wide QRS (left bundle branch block) at 70 per minute; S1, P2 and A2 are labelled. Expiration: P2 comes first and A2 about 50 ms later (reversed order, audible split). Inspiration: P2 moves later and fuses with the delayed A2, so a single S2 is heard. Paradoxical splitting: LBBB, RV pacing, severe aortic stenosis, obstructive HCM.
pe-phono-split-s2-paradoxical.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
pe-phono-split-s2-paradoxical.caption: Paradoxical (reversed) splitting of S2: A2 is delayed beyond P2, so the split is heard on expiration and disappears on inspiration; here with a wide-QRS (LBBB) reference ECG. Schematic, not a real recording.
pe-phono-split-s2-paradoxical.title: Paradoxical (reversed) splitting of S2 (LBBB)

pe-phono-split-s2-physiologic.alt_text: Schematic phonocardiogram in two panels, Expiration and Inspiration, each with a reference ECG at 70 per minute; S1, A2 and P2 are labelled. Expiration: A2 and P2 are about 20 ms apart, heard as one sound. Inspiration: P2 is later (about 55 ms after A2) and A2 slightly earlier, so the split is audible. Physiological splitting of S2 (best at the pulmonary area).
pe-phono-split-s2-physiologic.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
pe-phono-split-s2-physiologic.caption: Physiological splitting of S2: on expiration A2 and P2 are almost fused (heard as a single S2); on inspiration P2 moves later and the split widens. Schematic, not a real recording.
pe-phono-split-s2-physiologic.title: Physiological splitting of S2

pe-phono-split-s2-wide-fixed-asd.alt_text: Schematic phonocardiogram in two panels, Expiration and Inspiration, each with a reference ECG at 70 per minute; S1, A2 and P2 are labelled. In both panels A2 and P2 are about 60 ms apart: the split is wide and does not change with respiration (fixed). A soft, short crescendo-decrescendo ejection murmur sits in mid-systole (increased flow across the pulmonary valve). Wide fixed splitting + pulmonary flow murmur: atrial septal defect.
pe-phono-split-s2-wide-fixed-asd.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
pe-phono-split-s2-wide-fixed-asd.caption: Wide, fixed splitting of S2 with a soft pulmonary ejection (flow) murmur: secundum atrial septal defect. Schematic, not a real recording.
pe-phono-split-s2-wide-fixed-asd.title: Wide, fixed splitting of S2 (atrial septal defect)

pe-phono-vsd.alt_text: Schematic phonocardiogram under a reference ECG at 70 per minute, two cycles; S1 and S2 are labelled. S1 is of normal intensity. A loud, high-amplitude plateau murmur fills the whole of systole from S1 to S2 (holosystolic), louder than the heart sounds. Diastole is silent. Loud harsh holosystolic murmur: restrictive (small) ventricular septal defect at the left lower sternal border (grade 4 or more = palpable thrill).
pe-phono-vsd.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
pe-phono-vsd.caption: Restrictive ventricular septal defect: a loud, harsh holosystolic murmur from S1 to S2, maximal at the left lower sternal border, usually with a thrill. Schematic, not a real recording.
pe-phono-vsd.title: Ventricular septal defect: harsh holosystolic murmur

pe-pulse-alternans.alt_text: Schematic arterial pressure tracing (mmHg) under a reference ECG. The rhythm is regular at 84 per minute (equal RR intervals), but the systolic pressure alternates beat by beat between about 125 and 108 mmHg (strong, weak, strong, weak) with the same diastolic pressure. Pulsus alternans of severe LV systolic dysfunction; distinguish it from pulsus bigeminus, where the weak beat comes early (a premature beat).
pe-pulse-alternans.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
pe-pulse-alternans.caption: Pulsus alternans: regular rhythm with alternating strong and weak beats, a sign of severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction. Schematic, not a real tracing.
pe-pulse-alternans.title: Pulsus alternans (severe LV systolic dysfunction)

pe-pulse-bisferiens.alt_text: Schematic arterial pressure tracing (mmHg) under a reference ECG at 70 per minute. Pulsus bisferiens: each beat rises steeply to a first systolic peak (percussion wave), dips in mid-systole and rises again to a second peak of similar height (tidal wave), both peaks within systole and before the dicrotic notch; wide pulse pressure 150/60 mmHg. Classic in severe aortic regurgitation or combined aortic regurgitation and stenosis.
pe-pulse-bisferiens.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
pe-pulse-bisferiens.caption: Pulsus bisferiens: two systolic peaks (percussion and tidal waves) with a mid-systolic dip, felt in significant aortic regurgitation (alone or with aortic stenosis) and sometimes in obstructive HCM. Schematic, not a real tracing.
pe-pulse-bisferiens.title: Pulsus bisferiens (aortic regurgitation, mixed aortic valve disease)

pe-pulse-collapsing.alt_text: Schematic arterial pressure tracing (mmHg) under a reference ECG at 70 per minute. Collapsing or water-hammer pulse: a very steep upstroke to a high, sharp systolic peak of 170 mmHg reached about 75 ms after the upstroke, then a rapid collapse without a distinct dicrotic notch and a long diastolic run-off to a low diastolic pressure of 45 mmHg (pulse pressure 125 mmHg). Typical of chronic severe aortic regurgitation.
pe-pulse-collapsing.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
pe-pulse-collapsing.caption: Collapsing (water-hammer, Corrigan) pulse: a very rapid upstroke to a high peak and an abrupt collapse, with a wide pulse pressure; the pulse of chronic severe aortic regurgitation (also high-output states and a large PDA). Schematic, not a real tracing.
pe-pulse-collapsing.title: Collapsing (water-hammer) pulse (severe aortic regurgitation)

pe-pulse-jerky-hcm.alt_text: Schematic arterial pressure tracing (mmHg) under a reference ECG at 70 per minute. Each beat has a brisk, early, sharp upstroke peaking at 130 mmHg about 60 ms after the upstroke (spike), a mid-systolic fall to about 110 mmHg as dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction develops, then a smaller second rise (dome, about 120 mmHg) before the dicrotic notch; 130/75 mmHg. Jerky, spike-and-dome pulse of obstructive HCM, unlike the slow-rising pulse of aortic stenosis.
pe-pulse-jerky-hcm.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
pe-pulse-jerky-hcm.caption: Spike-and-dome (jerky) pulse of obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: a brisk early spike, a mid-systolic fall as the outflow tract obstructs, then a smaller late dome. Schematic, not a real tracing.
pe-pulse-jerky-hcm.title: Jerky (spike-and-dome) pulse of obstructive HCM

pe-pulse-normal.alt_text: Schematic arterial pressure tracing (mmHg) under a reference ECG at 70 per minute. Each beat has a brisk upstroke beginning just after the QRS, a rounded peak about 90 ms after the upstroke, a gentle decline, the dicrotic notch (labelled notch) at aortic valve closure about 300 ms after the upstroke followed by the small dicrotic wave, then a smooth diastolic run-off; 120/80 mmHg. The reference against which the abnormal pulse contours of this pack are compared.
pe-pulse-normal.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
pe-pulse-normal.caption: Normal arterial pulse for comparison: brisk upstroke, rounded peak early in systole, dicrotic notch at aortic valve closure. Schematic, not a real tracing.
pe-pulse-normal.title: Normal arterial pulse

pe-pulse-paradoxus.alt_text: Schematic arterial pressure tracing (mmHg) over 8 seconds with a respiration trace (shaded bands = inspiration) and a reference ECG at 96 per minute, regular. Pulsus paradoxus: the systolic pressure is about 113 mmHg in expiration and falls to about 92 mmHg during each inspiration (a fall of about 21 mmHg, abnormal when more than 10 mmHg), recovering on expiration, while the ECG rhythm stays regular. Classic sign of cardiac tamponade; also severe asthma/COPD, massive pulmonary embolism, hypovolaemic shock.
pe-pulse-paradoxus.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
pe-pulse-paradoxus.caption: Pulsus paradoxus: an exaggerated inspiratory fall in systolic pressure (more than 10 mmHg), classic in cardiac tamponade; shaded bands mark inspiration on the respiration trace. Schematic, not a real tracing.
pe-pulse-paradoxus.title: Pulsus paradoxus (cardiac tamponade)

pe-pulse-parvus-et-tardus.alt_text: Schematic arterial pressure tracing (mmHg) under a reference ECG, three beats at 70 per minute. Pulsus parvus et tardus of severe aortic stenosis: the upstroke rises slowly with an anacrotic shoulder (a notch-like hesitation) part-way up, reaches a rounded late peak about 250 ms after the upstroke, and the pulse pressure is narrow (105/80 mmHg). The dicrotic notch is small. Compare the normal pulse, which peaks about 90 ms after the upstroke.
pe-pulse-parvus-et-tardus.attribution: Original schematic generated for this study aid.
pe-pulse-parvus-et-tardus.caption: Pulsus parvus et tardus: a small, slow-rising carotid pulse with a late peak and an anacrotic shoulder on the upstroke, the pulse of severe valvular aortic stenosis. Schematic, not a real tracing.

preload-venous-return.alt_text: Left: four boxes - blood volume, venous tone (sympathetic), skeletal-muscle pump and respiratory pump - feed into mean systemic filling pressure (~7 mmHg), which drives flow to the right heart and sets RA pressure, RVEDV and LVEDV (preload). Right: the Guyton venous return curve falls as right atrial pressure rises, crossing zero flow near +7 mmHg (the x-intercept equals mean systemic filling pressure).
preload-venous-return.caption: Blood volume, venous tone and the muscle/respiratory pumps set mean systemic filling pressure, which drives venous return and so end-diastolic volume. Right: the venous return curve.

options.label: CTPA contraindicated (pregnancy, severe CKD, contrast allergy)

ctpa.text: CT pulmonary angiography (anticoagulation already started if probability is high or intermediate). Result?

ddimer.hint: Age-adjusted cut-off: ESC 2019 IIa B. Use a high-sensitivity assay. D-dimer is not used when clinical probability is high.
ddimer.text: D-dimer below the cut-off? (age-adjusted after 50 y: age x 10 µg/L)

ih-course.text: Intermediate-high risk on anticoagulation and monitoring: does the patient deteriorate haemodynamically?

low-rv.hint: ESC 2019: a patient with sPESI 0 but RV dysfunction or a positive biomarker is classed intermediate-low, not low.

options.label: Yes: RV dysfunction or troponin raised

low-rv.text: sPESI 0: was RV dysfunction or a raised troponin found (if assessed)?

lysis-ci.hint: Absolute (ESC 2019): previous haemorrhagic stroke or stroke of unknown origin; ischaemic stroke in last 6 months; CNS neoplasm; major trauma, surgery or head injury in last 3 weeks; bleeding diathesis; active bleeding.
lysis-ci.text: High-risk PE. Any contraindication to systemic thrombolysis?

perc.text: All 8 PERC criteria negative? (age <50, HR <100, SaO2 ≥95%, no haemoptysis, no oestrogen use, no prior VTE, no unilateral leg swelling, no surgery/trauma in 4 weeks)

ptp.hint: Use Wells (two-level) or revised Geneva. Start anticoagulation while waiting for tests if probability is high or intermediate (ESC 2019, I C).

options.label: Very low by gestalt: apply PERC

r-alt-imaging.cite: ESC 2019; AHA/ACC 2026 (YEARS useful in pregnancy; LMWH or UFH in pregnancy)
r-alt-imaging.detail:
- **V/Q scan**: a normal perfusion scan excludes PE; a high-probability scan confirms it.
- **Compression ultrasound**: proximal DVT in a patient with suspected PE is enough to start treatment.
- **Pregnancy**: D-dimer with pregnancy-adapted YEARS; leg ultrasound first if leg symptoms; then CTPA or perfusion scan (both deliver low fetal radiation). Treat with **LMWH** (DOACs and VKA are avoided in pregnancy).
r-alt-imaging.text: Use V/Q (perfusion) scanning or leg compression ultrasound; in pregnancy follow a pregnancy-adapted pathway.

r-embolectomy.cite: ESC 2019 (embolectomy I C; catheter therapy IIa C; ECMO IIb C); AHA/ACC 2026
r-embolectomy.detail:
- **Surgical pulmonary embolectomy**: ESC 2019 **I C** when thrombolysis is contraindicated or has failed.
- **Percutaneous catheter-directed treatment** (thrombectomy, low-dose local lysis): ESC 2019 **IIa C**, by local expertise.
- **VA-ECMO** may be considered in refractory circulatory collapse or arrest, combined with surgical or catheter therapy (ESC 2019 IIb C; AHA/ACC 2026: reasonable in refractory cardiogenic shock).
- Activate the PE response team (ESC 2019 IIa C; AHA/ACC 2026 recommended).
r-embolectomy.text: Thrombolysis contraindicated or failed: surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed therapy; ECMO as a bridge in refractory shock.

r-excluded.cite: ESC 2019 (age-adjusted and probability-adapted D-dimer IIa B)
r-excluded.detail:
- PERC-negative with very low gestalt, a negative D-dimer below the appropriate cut-off, or a negative CTPA safely rule out PE in that probability group.
- **Caution**: with high clinical probability and a negative CTPA, further testing may be considered (ESC 2019).
- Re-evaluate if symptoms persist or new features appear.
r-excluded.text: PE excluded (or testing not needed): no anticoagulation; look for another diagnosis.

r-int-high.cite: ESC 2019 (III B for routine thrombolysis); AHA/ACC 2026 (Category C3/D)
r-int-high.detail:
- PEITHO: full-dose thrombolysis reduced haemodynamic decompensation but increased major bleeding and haemorrhagic stroke, so it is **not routine** (ESC 2019 **III B**).
- Monitor in HDU/ICU; plan **rescue reperfusion** if the patient deteriorates.
- Involve the PE response team. AHA/ACC 2026: the benefit of catheter-directed therapy is unclear in Category C; in Category D (incipient failure: transient hypotension or normotensive shock) systemic thrombolysis (if bleeding risk is acceptable) or catheter-directed therapy may be considered.
- Switch to an oral anticoagulant once stable.
r-int-high.text: Intermediate-high risk, stable: anticoagulate (LMWH initially), monitor closely for 2-3 days; no routine thrombolysis.

r-int-low.cite: ESC 2019 (no routine thrombolysis, III B); AHA/ACC 2026 (Category C)
r-int-low.detail:
- Anticoagulation with LMWH (or a DOAC); ward-level care.
- **Routine primary systemic thrombolysis is not recommended** in intermediate- or low-risk PE (ESC 2019 **III B**).
- AHA/ACC 2026: Category C (elevated severity score; C1 normal RV and biomarkers, C2 abnormal RV or biomarker, C3 both) - hospitalise and anticoagulate; the benefit of catheter-directed therapy is unclear.
r-int-low.text: Intermediate-low risk: admit and anticoagulate; no routine thrombolysis.

r-low.cite: ESC 2019 (DOAC I A; early discharge IIa A); AHA/ACC 2026 (Category A-B)
r-low.detail:
- **DOAC preferred over VKA** (ESC 2019 I A; AHA/ACC 2026). Apixaban or rivaroxaban can start without parenteral lead-in; dabigatran and edoxaban need ≥5 days of heparin first.
- Avoid DOACs in severe renal impairment, pregnancy and lactation, and antiphospholipid syndrome.
- **Early discharge** in carefully selected low-risk patients (ESC 2019 **IIa A**): sPESI 0 or negative Hestia, no serious comorbidity, reliable follow-up. AHA/ACC 2026: Category A (asymptomatic) and B (symptomatic, low severity score) can be treated as outpatients.
- **Duration**: at least 3 months; stop if the PE was provoked by a major transient risk factor; extend if unprovoked or a persistent risk factor exists.
r-low.text: Low-risk PE: oral anticoagulation (DOAC); early discharge/home treatment if criteria met.

r-lysis.detail:
- **Systemic thrombolysis** for high-risk PE: ESC 2019 **I B**. Typical regimens: alteplase **100 mg over 2 h** (or 0.6 mg/kg over 15 min, max 50 mg, in extremis); streptokinase 1.5 million IU over 2 h (accelerated).
- **UFH** (weight-adjusted bolus then infusion) rather than LMWH in unstable patients or when reperfusion is planned.
- **Haemodynamics**: norepinephrine for hypotension (dobutamine for low output); only cautious fluid (≤500 mL) because the RV is pressure-overloaded; avoid intubation if possible (positive pressure and induction can cause arrest).
- Benefit is greatest within 48 h of symptoms but thrombolysis can help up to 6-14 days.
- AHA/ACC 2026: Category E1 (persistent hypotension with cardiogenic shock) - systemic thrombolysis is recommended (Class 1); catheter-directed therapy or mechanical/surgical thrombectomy are reasonable alternatives; PERT assessment is recommended for categories C-E.
r-lysis.text: High-risk PE: systemic thrombolysis plus UFH, with haemodynamic support.

r-other-shock.detail: A normal RV on bedside echo practically excludes PE as the cause of haemodynamic collapse (ESC 2019). Look for tamponade, ACS with LV failure, acute valve dysfunction, aortic dissection, hypovolaemia, sepsis, tension pneumothorax.
r-other-shock.text: PE is unlikely to explain the shock: look for another cause.

r-rescue.detail:
- **Rescue systemic thrombolysis**: ESC 2019 **I B**.
- Alternatives if bleeding risk is high: surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed treatment (ESC 2019 IIa C).
- Switch LMWH to UFH around reperfusion; norepinephrine for hypotension.
r-rescue.text: Deterioration on anticoagulation: rescue reperfusion now.

rvtrop.text: sPESI ≥1: RV dysfunction (echo or CTPA) AND a raised troponin?

spesi.hint: sPESI, 1 point each: age >80; cancer; chronic heart failure or chronic lung disease; HR ≥110; SBP <100; SaO2 <90%.
spesi.text: Confirmed, stable PE: what is the sPESI (or PESI class)?

start.hint: ESC 2019 instability: cardiac arrest; obstructive shock (SBP <90 or vasopressors needed, with hypoperfusion); or persistent hypotension (SBP <90 or a drop ≥40 mmHg for >15 min, not from another cause).
start.text: Suspected acute PE. Is the patient haemodynamically unstable?

tte.hint: RV/LV ratio ≥1.0, TAPSE <16 mm, McConnell sign, 60/60 sign, flattened septum, mobile right-heart thrombus.
tte.text: Bedside echocardiography: is there RV dysfunction?

unstable-ct.text: Start UFH now. Is CTPA immediately available and can the patient be moved safely?

years.text: How many YEARS items? (clinical signs of DVT; haemoptysis; PE the most likely diagnosis)

pulmonary-embolism-algorithm.alt_text: Decision tree for suspected pulmonary embolism. If unstable, CTPA or bedside echo for RV dysfunction leads to systemic thrombolysis, or surgical embolectomy or catheter therapy when thrombolysis is contraindicated. If stable, clinical probability decides between PERC, D-dimer (age-adjusted or YEARS thresholds) and CTPA. Confirmed PE is risk-stratified: sPESI 0 without RV dysfunction is low risk (DOAC, early discharge); sPESI 1 or more with RV dysfunction and raised troponin is intermediate-high (anticoagulation, monitoring, rescue thrombolysis if deterioration); others are intermediate-low.
pulmonary-embolism-algorithm.attribution: Based on the 2019 ESC acute PE guidelines and the 2026 AHA/ACC acute PE guideline; drawn for this app.
pulmonary-embolism-algorithm.caption: Decision tree for suspected acute PE: unstable patients go straight to echo or CTPA and reperfusion; stable patients pass through clinical probability (Wells, Geneva, PERC, YEARS), D-dimer and CTPA, then ESC 2019 risk classes built from sPESI, RV dysfunction and troponin, with AHA/ACC 2026 categories noted. Study aid based on the cited guidelines; verify against the current full guideline before clinical use.
pulmonary-embolism-algorithm.title: Acute pulmonary embolism: diagnosis, risk stratification and reperfusion

pv-loop.alt_text: Left ventricular pressure-volume loop running counter-clockwise: mitral closure at end-diastole (~120 mL, ~8 mmHg), isovolumic contraction up to aortic opening (~80 mmHg), ejection leftward to aortic closure / end-systole (~50 mL, ~120 mmHg), isovolumic relaxation down to mitral opening, then filling back to end-diastole. A green straight end-systolic pressure-volume relationship (ESPVR, slope Ees) touches the top-left corner; a blue end-diastolic pressure-volume relationship (EDPVR) curves up at high volumes. Loop width equals stroke volume = EDV minus ESV.
pv-loop.attribution: Original schematic, after Braunwald's Heart Disease and Klabunde.
pv-loop.caption: The LV pressure-volume loop: four phases, with ESPVR (slope = Ees, contractility) and EDPVR (passive compliance). Loop width = stroke volume.

raas-cascade.alt_text: Centre column: angiotensinogen from the liver is converted by renin (drug site 1, aliskiren) to angiotensin I, then by ACE (drug site 2, ACE inhibitor) to angiotensin II. Left: a box lists the triggers for renin release (low renal perfusion pressure, low sodium chloride at the macula densa, and beta-1 sympathetic stimulation of the juxtaglomerular cells, drug site 6, beta-blocker), inhibited by angiotensin II and natriuretic peptides; a second box notes that ACE also inactivates bradykinin, so ACE inhibitors raise bradykinin and cause cough. Right: angiotensin II acts on the AT1 receptor (drug site 3, ARB or the valsartan in ARNI), causing vasoconstriction, efferent more than afferent arteriolar tone, aldosterone release, proximal sodium reabsorption, thirst and ADH release, increased sympathetic outflow, and hypertrophy and fibrosis. Below: angiotensin II and high potassium release aldosterone, which acts on the mineralocorticoid receptor in collecting-duct principal cells (drug site 4, MRA) to retain sodium, excrete potassium and promote fibrosis. Bottom: ANP from the atria and BNP from the ventricles cause natriuresis, vasodilatation and lower renin, aldosterone and sympathetic tone; neprilysin degrades them (drug site 5, sacubitril), and NT-proBNP is not a neprilysin substrate.
raas-cascade.attribution: Original schematic, after Guyton & Hall, Berne & Levy and Braunwald's Heart Disease.
raas-cascade.caption: Renin is the rate-limiting step; angiotensin II acts through AT1; aldosterone acts on the mineralocorticoid receptor; natriuretic peptides are the brake and neprilysin removes them. Numbers mark where each drug class acts.
raas-cascade.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 480" role="img" aria-label="Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone cascade with natriuretic peptides and drug sites" style="color:var(--ink)"><title>RAAS cascade and drug sites</title><desc>Angiotensinogen from the liver is cleaved by renin to angiotensin I, which ACE converts to angiotensin II. Renin release rises with low renal perfusion pressure, low sodium chloride at the macula densa and beta-1 sympathetic stimulation. ACE also inactivates bradykinin. Angiotensin II acts on AT1 receptors causing vasoconstriction, efferent arteriolar constriction, aldosterone release, proximal sodium reabsorption, thirst and ADH release, sympathetic facilitation and hypertrophy and fibrosis. Aldosterone, also released by high potassium, acts on mineralocorticoid receptors in the collecting duct. ANP and BNP oppose the system and are degraded by neprilysin. Numbered drug sites: 1 aliskiren at renin, 2 ACE inhibitor at ACE, 3 ARB at AT1, 4 MRA at the mineralocorticoid receptor, 5 sacubitril at neprilysin, 6 beta-blocker at the beta-1 receptor of the juxtaglomerular reentry-circuit.alt_text: A vertical ring of conducting tissue around a central obstacle. An impulse enters from the top and leaves at the bottom toward the rest of the heart. The left limb is the alpha pathway, fast with a long effective refractory period; a red bar marks unidirectional block in it near the top. The right limb is the beta pathway, slow with a short refractory period. Chevrons show the impulse travelling down the beta pathway and back up the alpha pathway, and a moving dot circulates around the loop. Text lists the three requirements, the wavelength rule (conduction velocity times refractory period must be shorter than the circuit) and examples: AV nodal re-entry, AV re-entry using an accessory pathway, typical atrial flutter and scar-related VT.
reentry-circuit.attribution: Original schematic, after Braunwald's Heart Disease and Zipes & Jalife.
reentry-circuit.caption: Re-entry needs a circuit around an obstacle, unidirectional block in one limb and slow conduction in the other. A premature beat blocks in the fast pathway (long ERP), goes down the slow pathway and re-enters the recovered fast pathway retrogradely.

reentry-circuit.title: Re-entry circuit

adenosine.hint: Record a rhythm strip during the push. Warn the patient (chest tightness, flushing). Caution: severe asthma; reduce dose with dipyridamole, heart transplant, central line.

options.label: Transient AV block revealed flutter waves or atrial tachycardia (rhythm continues)

adenosine.text: Give adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push with a saline flush (then 12 mg; ESC lists 6-18 mg). What happened?

options.label: Irregular (AF, flutter with variable block, multifocal atrial tachycardia)

r-ccb.cite: AHA 2025 Adult ALS (diltiazem/verapamil 2a B-R; cardioversion 1 B-NR); ESC 2019 SVT (IIa).
r-ccb.detail:
- AHA 2025: IV diltiazem or verapamil can be effective for stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia (COR 2a, B-R); synchronized cardioversion when vagal and drug therapy fail or are contraindicated (COR 1, B-NR).
- ESC 2019: verapamil/diltiazem class IIa; IV beta-blocker class IIa.
- Avoid non-dihydropyridine CCB with hypotension, HFrEF, or any suspicion of pre-excitation or VT.
r-ccb.text: IV verapamil or diltiazem (or an IV beta-blocker); synchronized cardioversion if drugs fail

r-irregular-narrow.detail:
- Multifocal atrial tachycardia (>=3 P-wave morphologies): treat the underlying lung disease, hypoxia, electrolytes; cardioversion does not work.
- Adenosine is not useful for AF.
r-irregular-narrow.text: Irregular narrow-complex tachycardia: manage as AF (rate control, anticoagulation decision) - see the AF decision guide

r-irregular-wide.cite: AHA 2025 Adult ALS (3: Harm C-LD); ESC 2019 SVT (pre-excited AF).
r-irregular-wide.detail:
- AHA 2025: adenosine should not be given for haemodynamically unstable, irregularly irregular, or polymorphic wide-complex tachycardia (COR 3: Harm, C-LD).
- Pre-excited AF: procainamide or ibutilide, or electrical cardioversion; then accessory-pathway ablation.
- AF with known stable BBB (identical QRS in sinus rhythm) is managed as AF.
r-irregular-wide.text: Irregular wide-complex tachycardia: suspect pre-excited AF (or AF with bundle branch block). No adenosine or AV-nodal blockers; cardioversion

r-poly.cite: AHA 2025 Adult ALS (Mg 2b C-LD with long QT; routine Mg with normal QT 3: No benefit C-LD); ESC 2022 ventricular arrhythmias. Magnesium dose is a typical value.
r-poly.detail:
- Torsades de pointes (long QT): IV magnesium sulphate (typically 2 g), K+ to high-normal, remove QT-prolonging drugs; overdrive pacing or isoprenaline for pause- or bradycardia-dependent torsades.
- Polymorphic VT with normal QT is usually acute ischaemia: treat as ACS.
- Polymorphic VT is usually unstable: defibrillation (unsynchronized) energy.
- AHA 2025: magnesium may be considered for recurrent polymorphic VT with a long QT (COR 2b, C-LD); **routine** magnesium for polymorphic VT with a normal QT is not recommended (COR 3: No benefit, C-LD).
r-poly.text: Polymorphic VT: defibrillate if unstable or pulseless; torsades -> IV magnesium, correct potassium, stop QT-prolonging drugs; ischaemia -> urgent angiography

r-svt-ab.cite: ESC 2019 SVT (adenosine IIa C in WCT without pre-excitation); AHA 2025 Adult ALS.
r-svt-ab.detail:
- ESC 2019: adenosine is a reasonable option for wide-QRS tachycardia when there is no pre-excitation on the resting ECG (IIa, C).
- Comparison with a sinus-rhythm ECG showing the same QRS morphology is the strongest evidence for aberrancy.
- Still no verapamil or diltiazem unless VT is truly excluded.
r-svt-ab.text: SVT with aberrancy is reasonable to treat as SVT (vagal manoeuvres, adenosine); if it does not terminate, treat as VT

r-sync-cv.cite: AHA 2025 Adult ALS (sync cardioversion COR 1 B-NR); ESC 2019 SVT (class I).
r-sync-cv.detail:
- AHA 2025: synchronized cardioversion is recommended for haemodynamically unstable narrow- or wide-complex tachycardia (COR 1, B-NR).
- ESC 2019 SVT: haemodynamically unstable patients -> synchronized DC cardioversion (class I).
- Use the device's recommended energy; irregular **polymorphic** wide-complex rhythm = unsynchronized defibrillation dose.
- A regular narrow-complex rhythm may be given adenosine **only** if it does not delay cardioversion.

r-term.cite: AHA 2025 Adult ALS (COR 1 B-R vagal and adenosine); ESC 2019 SVT (adenosine I B; ablation first-line).
r-term.detail:
- AHA 2025: vagal manoeuvres (COR 1, B-R) and adenosine (COR 1, B-R) for regular narrow-complex tachycardia.
- ESC 2019: adenosine 6-18 mg IV bolus is class I (B); vagal manoeuvres first-line.
- Look for pre-excitation (short PR, delta wave) in sinus rhythm: WPW changes management.
- Recurrent symptomatic AVNRT/AVRT: catheter ablation is first-line (ESC 2019).
r-term.text: AV-node-dependent re-entry (AVNRT or AVRT) likely: record a sinus-rhythm 12-lead ECG and refer for catheter ablation if recurrent

r-unmasked.cite: ESC 2019 SVT; ESC 2024 AF (flutter anticoagulation as for AF).
r-unmasked.detail:
- Adenosine is diagnostic here, not therapeutic: atrial activity continues during AV block.
- Typical flutter (sawtooth waves, atrial ~300/min, often 2:1 = ventricular ~150 bpm): cavotricuspid isthmus ablation is highly effective.
- Anticoagulate flutter like AF.
r-unmasked.text: Atrial flutter or atrial tachycardia unmasked: control rate, assess stroke risk as in AF, and plan cardioversion or ablation

r-vt.cite: ESC 2019 SVT (procainamide IIa, amiodarone IIb); AHA 2025 Adult ALS (antiarrhythmics 2b B-R; cardioversion 1 B-NR; verapamil/diltiazem 3: Harm B-NR).
r-vt.detail:
- ESC 2019: procainamide should be considered (IIa) and is prioritised over amiodarone (IIb) (PROCAMIO).
- AHA 2025: IV amiodarone, procainamide or sotalol may be considered (COR 2b, B-R); synchronized cardioversion when drugs fail (COR 1, B-NR).
- AHA 2025: verapamil and diltiazem should not be given for wide-complex tachycardia (COR 3: Harm, B-NR) - risk of haemodynamic collapse in VT.
- After termination: echo, ischaemia evaluation, electrolytes, and assessment for ICD (ESC 2022 ventricular arrhythmias).
r-vt.text: Stable monomorphic VT: IV procainamide (or amiodarone); synchronized cardioversion if drugs fail or the patient deteriorates. Never verapamil

r-vt-uncertain.cite: AHA 2025 Adult ALS (adenosine 2b B-NR; verapamil/diltiazem 3: Harm B-NR).
r-vt-uncertain.detail:
- AHA 2025: in stable regular monomorphic WCT, IV adenosine may be considered for treatment or rhythm diagnosis (COR 2b, B-NR).
- Misdiagnosing VT as SVT and giving verapamil can be fatal; misdiagnosing SVT as VT and giving procainamide or cardioversion is safe.
- Algorithms (Brugada, Vereckei aVR) help but none is perfect; clinical history (prior MI, structural disease) is the strongest single predictor.
r-vt-uncertain.text: When in doubt, treat as VT. Adenosine may be tried for diagnosis only if regular, monomorphic and stable; otherwise procainamide/amiodarone or cardioversion

options.label: Unstable: hypotension, shock, altered mental status, ischaemic chest pain, acute HF

unstable.text: Tachycardia with a pulse (rate typically 150 bpm or more when it causes symptoms). Is there instability caused by the arrhythmia?

vagal.hint: Carotid sinus massage only without carotid bruit or prior stroke/TIA. Modified Valsalva roughly doubles success vs standard Valsalva (REVERT).
vagal.text: Regular narrow-complex: perform vagal manoeuvres (modified Valsalva: strain for 15 s, then lie flat with legs raised). Did it terminate?

vt-clues.hint: VT clues: AV dissociation, fusion or capture beats, precordial concordance, QRS >160 ms, northwest axis, prior MI. A history of MI makes VT most likely.

options.label: VT features or structural heart disease (prior MI, cardiomyopathy)
Known BBB or aberrancy with identical QRS in sinus rhythm, no structural heart disease

vt-clues.text: Regular monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia: assume VT unless proven otherwise. Which fits best?

regular-tachycardia-algorithm.alt_text: Decision tree for tachycardia with a pulse. It decides between synchronized cardioversion for instability, vagal manoeuvres then adenosine then calcium-channel blocker for regular narrow-complex tachycardia, and VT-first management of wide-complex tachycardia, including irregular and polymorphic wide rhythms.
regular-tachycardia-algorithm.attribution: Based on the 2025 AHA Adult Advanced Life Support guidelines and the 2019 ESC SVT guidelines; drawn for this app.
regular-tachycardia-algorithm.caption: Decision tree for tachycardia with a pulse: unstable -> synchronized cardioversion; narrow regular -> vagal manoeuvres, adenosine, CCB; wide -> VT until proven otherwise, never verapamil. Study aid based on the cited guidelines; verify against the current full guideline before clinical use.
regular-tachycardia-algorithm.title: Tachycardia with a pulse: narrow vs wide complex

s2-splitting.alt_text: A grid of four rows and two columns, expiration and inspiration, each cell showing S1 then the components of S2 on a time line. Normal physiological splitting: a single S2 in expiration, A2 then P2 separated in inspiration. Wide splitting, as in right bundle branch block, pulmonary stenosis, mitral regurgitation or VSD: A2 and P2 separated in expiration and further apart in inspiration. Fixed splitting in atrial septal defect: the same wide gap in both phases. Paradoxical or reversed splitting in left bundle branch block, RV pacing, severe aortic stenosis or HCM: P2 comes before A2 in expiration and the two fuse into a single sound in inspiration.
s2-splitting.attribution: Original schematic, after Braunwald's Heart Disease.
s2-splitting.caption: A2 (red) and P2 (blue) in expiration vs inspiration. Normal: split only on inspiration. Wide: split throughout, wider on inspiration. Fixed (ASD): the same in both. Paradoxical: split on expiration, single on inspiration.

s2-splitting.title: S2 splitting patterns

arr-q.text: Suspected arrhythmic syncope. Does the ECG show bifascicular block (RBBB plus left anterior or posterior fascicular block, or LBBB)?

options.label: Structural or cardiopulmonary disease (AS, HCM, MI, PE, dissection)
Arrhythmic syncope (palpitations, conduction disease, family history of sudden death)

hr-type.text: High risk: early intensive evaluation in the ED/syncope unit or admission. What is the main suspicion?

initial.hint: Orthostatic hypotension (ESC 2018): sustained fall in SBP >=20 mmHg or DBP >=10 mmHg, or SBP to <90 mmHg, on standing.

options.label: Diagnostic arrhythmia or cardiac cause on ECG/monitoring

initial.text: Initial evaluation: history (with eyewitness), examination including supine and standing BP, and a 12-lead ECG. Is a diagnosis certain or highly likely?

r-cardiac-dx.cite: ESC 2018 syncope (diagnostic criteria for arrhythmic syncope).
r-cardiac-dx.detail:
- ECG findings that are diagnostic (ESC 2018): persistent sinus bradycardia <40 bpm or pauses >3 s while awake, Mobitz II or third-degree AV block, alternating LBBB and RBBB, VT or rapid paroxysmal SVT, pacemaker malfunction with pauses.
- Structural causes: severe aortic stenosis, obstructive HCM, atrial myxoma, acute MI, PE, aortic dissection, tamponade.
r-cardiac-dx.text: Cardiac syncope diagnosed: admit and treat the cause (e.g., pacing for high-grade AV block, ICD/ablation for VT, valve or ischaemia treatment)

r-eps.cite: ESC 2018 syncope (EPS in unexplained syncope with bifascicular BBB; pacing after positive EPS class I); ESC 2021 pacing/CRT (HV >=70 ms; alternating BBB).
r-eps.detail:
- ESC 2018/2021: EPS is the next step when syncope with bifascicular BBB remains unexplained after non-invasive evaluation (class not listed here); pacing after a positive EPS was upgraded to class I in ESC 2018.
- ESC 2021 pacing: pacing is indicated with baseline HV >=70 ms, second- or third-degree intra- or infra-Hisian block during incremental atrial pacing, or an abnormal pharmacological challenge.
- Alternating bundle branch block: pacing indicated with or without symptoms (ESC 2021).
- Negative EPS: implantable loop recorder (ILR) to capture the next event.
r-eps.text: Electrophysiological study; pacemaker if HV interval is 70 ms or more or infra-Hisian block is provoked; otherwise an implantable loop recorder

r-exertional.cite: ESC 2018 syncope (exercise testing in exertional syncope).
r-exertional.detail:
- ESC 2018: exercise testing should be performed in patients with syncope during or shortly after exertion (after echo excludes severe outflow obstruction).
- **During** exertion = cardiac until proven otherwise; **after** exertion (post-exercise) is more often reflex.
- Young athlete: also consider ARVC and coronary anomalies (CT coronary angiography / cardiac MRI).
r-exertional.text: Syncope during exertion: exclude obstruction with echocardiography first, then exercise testing; think AS, HCM, anomalous coronary artery, CPVT, long QT type 1

r-intermediate.cite: ESC 2018 syncope (ED risk-based management, class I B); ACC/AHA/HRS 2017 syncope (observation protocols; risk scores).
r-intermediate.detail:
- ESC 2018: patients with neither high- nor low-risk features should be observed in the ED or a syncope unit instead of being hospitalised (the ED management recommendation is class I, B).
- ACC/AHA 2017: a structured ED observation protocol can be effective for intermediate-risk patients.
- Risk scores (San Francisco, OESIL, EGSYS, Canadian Syncope Risk Score) may support but should not replace clinical judgement.
r-intermediate.text: Neither high nor low risk: observation in an ED observation unit or syncope unit, or prompt expert outpatient review, rather than routine admission

r-low.cite: ESC 2018 syncope (ED discharge of low-risk patients, class I B); ACC/AHA/HRS 2017 syncope.
r-low.detail:
- ESC 2018: low-risk patients (likely reflex, situational or orthostatic) do not need further diagnostic tests in the ED and can be discharged (class I, B).
- Low-risk features: prodrome typical of reflex syncope (light-headedness, warmth, sweating, nausea), trigger (unpleasant sight, sound, smell or pain; prolonged standing; crowded hot place; during a meal; cough, micturition, defecation; head rotation), long history of similar recurrent episodes, no structural heart disease, normal examination and ECG.
- ACC/AHA 2017: outpatient management is reasonable for presumptive reflex syncope without serious medical conditions; routine comprehensive laboratory testing and routine neuro-imaging are not useful.
r-low.text: Low risk: discharge from the emergency department with education; no further hospital tests

r-monitor.cite: ESC 2018 syncope (in-hospital monitoring for high risk; ILR class I).
r-monitor.detail:
- ESC 2018: in-bed or telemetry monitoring is warranted in high-risk patients with suspected arrhythmic syncope.
- ILR (ESC 2018, class I): recurrent syncope of uncertain origin without high-risk criteria and a high likelihood of recurrence within battery life; and high-risk patients after a comprehensive non-diagnostic evaluation.
- Holter monitoring only helps when episodes are frequent (typically daily to weekly).
- Channelopathy clues (QTc prolongation, Brugada type 1 pattern, family history of sudden death) need specialist evaluation.
r-monitor.text: In-hospital ECG monitoring (telemetry) now; if unexplained, prolonged monitoring with an implantable loop recorder

r-nonsyncope.detail:
- Seizure clues: tongue biting (lateral), prolonged confusion after the event, head turning, tonic-clonic movements starting at onset, aura.
- Note: brief myoclonic jerks are common in syncope and do not prove epilepsy.
- Psychogenic pseudosyncope: long apparent unconsciousness, eyes closed, frequent episodes.
r-nonsyncope.text: Non-syncopal TLOC: evaluate the alternative cause (neurology, glucose, toxicology, head injury)

r-oh.cite: ESC 2018 syncope; ACC/AHA/HRS 2017 syncope. Classes not listed here.
r-oh.detail:
- Causes: drugs (vasodilators, diuretics, alpha-blockers, antidepressants), volume depletion, autonomic failure (diabetes, Parkinson disease, multiple system atrophy, amyloid).
- ESC 2018 measures: education, adequate hydration and salt intake, reduce hypotensive drugs, counter-pressure manoeuvres, abdominal binders or compression stockings, head-up tilt sleeping, midodrine or fludrocortisone.
- ACC/AHA 2017 adds droxidopa for neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.
- Delayed OH (beyond 3 minutes) and initial OH (within 15 s) exist; tilt testing helps when the active-standing test is negative.
r-oh.text: Orthostatic hypotension: remove offending drugs, correct volume, then non-pharmacological measures and, if needed, midodrine or fludrocortisone

r-reflex.cite: ESC 2018 syncope (reflex syncope treatment; carotid sinus massage >40 y). Classes not listed here.
r-reflex.detail:
- ESC 2018: education and reassurance are the cornerstone; counter-pressure manoeuvres (with tilt training if needed) in young patients with prodromes.
- Older hypertensive patients: reduce or stop hypotensive drugs, targeting SBP ~140 mmHg.
- Young patients with low-BP phenotype: fludrocortisone or midodrine may be considered.
- Older patients (typically >40 years) with dominant cardioinhibitory (asystolic) reflex syncope and severe unpredictable recurrences: dual-chamber pacing.
- Carotid sinus massage in patients >40 years with unexplained syncope compatible with a reflex mechanism (positive: pause >3 s and/or SBP fall >50 mmHg with symptoms).
r-reflex.text: Reflex (vasovagal/situational/carotid sinus) syncope: explain, reassure, avoid triggers, teach counter-pressure manoeuvres; no routine further tests

r-structural.cite: ESC 2018 syncope (echocardiography in suspected structural heart disease).
r-structural.detail:
- ESC 2018: echocardiography is indicated with known or suspected structural heart disease.
- Severe aortic stenosis with syncope -> aortic valve replacement; obstructive HCM -> avoid dehydration and vasodilators, consider septal reduction and ICD risk assessment.
- Acute MI, PE and aortic dissection can all present as syncope: treat as the primary emergency.
r-structural.text: Admit; echocardiography and cause-directed imaging (CT for PE or dissection), then treat the cause

risk.hint: High risk: exertional or supine syncope, sudden palpitations then syncope, new chest pain/dyspnoea/headache, severe structural or coronary disease, SBP <90, unexplained systolic murmur, GI bleeding, high-risk ECG.

options.label: Yes: at least one high-risk feature
Neither clearly high nor low risk

risk.text: Syncope of uncertain cause. Risk-stratify (ESC 2018): any high-risk feature?

options.label: No: seizure, trauma, intoxication, hypoglycaemia or psychogenic pseudosyncope suspected
Uncertain (e.g., unwitnessed): evaluate as syncope while excluding mimics

tloc.text: Transient loss of consciousness (TLOC). Is it syncope: rapid onset, short duration, loss of postural tone, spontaneous complete recovery, due to cerebral hypoperfusion?

syncope-algorithm.alt_text: Decision tree for syncope. It decides whether loss of consciousness is syncope, whether the initial evaluation gives a diagnosis (reflex, orthostatic, cardiac), and if not, the risk group that determines discharge, observation or admission, with next tests for structural, arrhythmic and exertional syncope.
syncope-algorithm.attribution: Based on the 2018 ESC syncope guidelines and the 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS syncope guideline; drawn for this app.
syncope-algorithm.caption: Decision tree for transient loss of consciousness: confirm syncope, make a diagnosis from history/standing BP/ECG, risk-stratify, and decide discharge, observation or admission with targeted tests. Study aid based on the cited guidelines; verify against the current full guideline before clinical use.
